speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the order for motions:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROTOCOL COVERING SUPPLIES TO BE FURNISHED BY THE UNITED STATES, THE UNITED KINGDOM AND CANADA
speechtext:
I should like to make a brief announcement with respect to Canadian supplies for the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. A protocol setting forth the supplies to be furnished to the U.S.S.R. by the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada is now under negotiation. The protocol will cover the supplies to be provided during the year beginning July 1, 1943. To avoid giving information which would be of great value to the enemy, the contents of the protocol must 
remain secret. It is expected that under it the three countries will undertake to make available for shipment to Russia stated quantities of munitions, war materials and essential supplies, subject to modification after consultation, in the event of unforeseen developments in the war situation.
Hitherto supplies have been furnished to the U.S.S.R. by the United Kingdom and the United States under annual agreements of this type to which the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union have been parties. The supplies which have gone to Russia from Canada, except for wheat and some miscellaneous commodities for which special arrangements were made, have been included in the commitments made by the United Kingdom or in some cases in those made by the United States. It has been agreed between the governments concerned that it is appropriate for Canada as an important producer of war supplies for the U.S.S.R. to become a direct party to the protocol now under negotiation. In this way Canada will be able to express once again her deep appreciation of the outstanding importance to the common cause of the contribution of the U.S.S.R. and her recognition of the vital importance of the Soviet front.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, May 10, consideration in committee of bill No. 76, for granting to his majesty aid for the purpose of making available Canadian war supplies to the united nations,-Mr. Usley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last evening I promised to give as much information about the use of the billion dollar gift as seemed desirable in the light of security considerations.
This is a very complicated matter, and before I present the tables which I have before me I wish to give a brief explanation of how we worked under the legislation and of some of the difficulties. I wish first to remind the committee that the legislation did not contemplate that we should purchase so many tanks, planes or guns, and so many bushels of wheat or pounds of cheese, and turn these physical commodities over to Great Britain. Had it done so it would have been far easier for us to give the specific information which now appears to be desired by the committee. On the contrary it contemplated the gift of Canadian dollars to be turned over to the British government to enable it to purchase in Canada certain munitions of war, raw materials and foodstuffs, and to defray certain, expenditures incurred by the British government in Canada arising out of the war. These dollars so made available were to supplement Britain's supply of dollars available from other sources for the same purposes. If members will examine the main operative provisions of the War Appropriation (United Kingdom Financing) Act, 1942, subsections 1 and 2 of section 3, they will find the wording to be as follows:
3. (1) The minister may, subject to regulations to be made by the governor in council with reference thereto, pay out of the consolidated revenue fund to the Bank of Canada for the account of the government of the United Kingdom-
Let me emphasize these words:
-a sum or sums of money not exceeding in the aggregate one thousand million dollars ($1,000,000,000), to enable it to purchase in Canada aircraft, tanks, mechanical transport vehicles, guns, ammunition and other munitions of war, foodstuffs,^ raw materials, and other commodities and supplies essential to the conduct of the war and the maintenance of the people of the United Kingdom, and to defray other expenses incurred in Canada arising out of the war.
(2) Payments or advances may be made under subsection one of this section from time to time upon the minister being satisfied that the amount thereof is necessary to make the said purchases and defray the said expenses.

These two subsections, it will be noted, indicated clearly (1) a mechanism; (2) a purpose, and (3) a procedure. The mechanism was the payment of dollars not exceeding one billion into the account of the government of the United Kingdom in the Bank of Canada. The purpose was to enable the United Kingdom to buy munitions, raw materials and foodstuffs in Canada and to defray other war expenditures in Canada, supplementing the other dollar resources of the United Kingdom, in order that her purchases of necessary war supplies and services in Canada would not be limited by any shortage of Canadian dollars. The procedure was that the Minister of Finance was to make payments or advances from the appropriation into Britain's account with the Bank of Canada from time to time upon his being satisfied that the amount of said payments or advances was necessary to make the said purchases and defray the said expenses. In accordance with these provisions and to meet these requirements we had to work out a rather complicated system of requisitions for advances, certificates of necessity, reports on expenditures made, statements and forecasts regarding balance of payments, and so forth.
It will I think be immediately apparent from what I have said that there are real difficulties in presenting to this committee the detailed information which the committee would like to have about the expenditure of the gift. The most obvious difficulty results from the fact that, when dollars from two or more sources are placed in a common fund, they lose their identity, and strictly speaking it is impossible to say that a dollar taken out of the common fund to meet a given expenditure comes from one source rather than another. It is therefore only by certain arbitrary assumptions that we can allot the use of the gift to the purchase of a certain group of eligible commodities or expenditures-eligible that is to say under the terms of the United Kingdom Financing Act-and not to a different combination of eligible commodities and expenditures. For instance, if we attribute to the gift all the munitions of war purchased by Britain in Canada during the period, we are necessarily forced to attribute the purchase of a smaller volume of foodstuffs and raw materials to the gift; and contrariwise, if we attribute to the gift all the foodstuffs and raw materials purchased by Britain in Canada during the period, we have less of the gift to attribute to the purchase of munitions.
Take also the case of freight payments which was mentioned last evening. These freight

Mutual Aid Bill
payments to the Canadian seaboard had to be made by or on behalf of Britain; and if we regard them as being paid out of the gift, it merely means that fewer dollars from the gift could be attributed to the purchase of, say, foodstuffs or raw materials. Apart from this, there is no significance at all in the problem.
Again, it should be clear from what I have said how difficult it is to translate dollar expenditures into physical quantities of munitions or raw materials, number of tanks or planes, tons of aluminum or copper or zinc, and so forth, even if we were willing to take all the risks from the security point of view. My specific point is this, that if, for instance, for the first week of last July the United Kingdom had requisitioned us for $20 million out of the gift appropriation, demonstrating that this amount was necessary to enable her to meet, with the dollars she had already in hand, the payments for Canadian purchases and for other Canadian expenditures which she had to make during that week, including, let us say, part of the cost of a shipment of aircraft or aircraft parts, part of a purchase due of bacon or cheese or wheat, some freight payments, and so forth, it is practically impossible to convert into terms of physical magnitude, x units of this, that and the other items, the purposes for which the funds were used.
Finally, I think it will also be clear to the committee that to require information in too great detail, and to have it presented in such a form as to be intelligible and not misleading, involves very complete disclosure of the business affairs and operations in this country of another government. This follows from the point I have already made, that only by very arbitrary assumptions can we attribute specific expenditures to the gift, advances out of which were credited to. the British bank account in the Bank of Canada.
Taking all these considerations into account, I have had certain tables prepared which go as far as I think is practicable in revealing to the committee the information which it would like to have, and I hope the committee will find them satisfactory under all the circumstances. I have had the tables mimeographed, and I will have them distributed to hon. members so that they will be able to follow them if they wish.

Let me make this clear in case there should be any mistake about it. We mean to hold our own. I have not become the king's first minister in order to preside over the liquidation of the British empire.

This bill and the bill of last year shows that Canada is not going to be talked out of the British empire. Canada will have to be fought out of the British empire before what was said the other day happens. If Canada could have been talked out it would have been done long ago. I shall not refer to the remarks of some of our friends from the province of Quebec. They have expressed their views and they have the right to express them. But I must tell them that they should try to see the cause and effect of all this. This fight down at Sussex did not originate the other day; it went back to the days of the South African war and the first world war. We must consider the cause and effect of the home defence remarks of some members from the province of Quebec yesterday and last Friday and on the stand of isolation taken in the past. We must consider the results of the plebiscite vote and the disunity it caused and all these other things. The country voted for a total war effort and. last year, acting on that, we gave a gift of a billion dollars. It was a gift, so-called, but it was of a very questionable nature, because Britain shared1 it in part with other allies. In some respects it was like a gift horse. It was not a total gift at all because the money given to Great Britain was used partly for the assistance of other suffering countries.
The spirit on the whole, though, of this bill is correct and I believe it will commend itself to the wisdom and judgment of the country. What was done last year had been delayed too long; it should have been done long ago. If Canada had taken this stand of aid and support to Britain at the last colonial conference in 1937 and had backed up New Zealand andi Australia, had told them that she was prepared to do this to the last man and the last dollar, we would have avoided this war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
I have one or two questions that I should like to ask the Minister of Finance, but I want to preface them with a few remarks which I think had better be made at this stage of the proceedings. I do not intend to answer the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). I hold no brief for those who have voted against this bill, but I never like to see anyone, whether he comes from Toronto or elsewhere, cast doubt upon the loyalty of Quebec simply because some people in this house do not share the same views. I voted for this measure last night and. I shall explain why I am for it, but just the same I do not think it is a fair procedure to say that, because some people from Quebec express different views, the province of Quebec does not understand how the war effort should be run and how things in Canada should be run for

Mutual Aid Bill
the war. This sort of attitude should be left aside. When an hon. member does not hear just exactly what he would like to hear he should not cast reflection upon the loyalty of others.
I voted for this measure for many reasons which in my judgment are sound and good and which I will be able to justify to my constituents when the time comes. I repeatedly told my people that I would support the government in all the aspects of its war policy except conscription for overseas service. I shall continue to support the government, because of all the political parties of one kind and another that we now have, I have the most confidence in the Liberal party. Of all the leaders of the different parties, and I have much esteem for some of them, I place the Prime Minister and leader of the government above all. I have the conviction that by weakening the position of the Prime Minister on any of thelse issues we may very well contribute to the formation of a political combination the very existence of which would endanger the success of the war effort so harmoniously achieved under the present administration, and would probably bring about exactly the opposite of what those who oppose t'he present measure desire.
I gave my second reason for supporting this measure when I spoke in this house on February 16. I should like to be permitted to quote the remarks I made on that occasion so that they may be taken with what I have to say to-day. They are reported on page 485 of Hansard of February 16, and read as follows:
When a measure of somewhat similar nature was presented to us last year in the form of a grant of one billion to the United Kingdom, I agreed to it because I felt that a country that had been spared the actual sacrifices of war on its own territory, a country that had not been invaded and trampled and massacred as had Russia and China, and a country that had not been subjected to the most horrible aerial warfare, as had Britain, could make further financial sacrifices as a sort of compensation, I may say, to those who had been in the path of the monster and who had delayed so much, as to render it nearly impossible now, his direct assault on us. Those were the motives which made me accept last year's proposal. The way in which it was presented and the poor and insufficient explanations given to the public were such that many still think we took one billion in gold from our treasury and gave it to Britain. What we did was to provide the tools of war for those who were in the front line of defence and could not pay for it. That money was spent in Canada, provided work for Canadians and used Canadian materials. What I did not like about it was the way in which it was done, handing everything to Great Britain, which took the credit for transferring afterwards part of it to China and Russia. If there is truth in what has been published in a Canadian paper lately, to the effect that part of it was directed
by Britain to Australia and New Zealand who paid Britain for it out of their credit balances in Britain, I like it less.
But the way in which the lease-lend appropriation is presented to-day should not provoke the same objections. It appears to be an improved, more dignified and more nationally conscious form of financial help to world freedom. The motives are the same as last year, but the method of doing it is greatly improved. We thereby take one more step to manifest our complete independence from and equality with Britain. We appear no more as the vassal bringing tribute but as the equal partner who puts his assets in a common pool with those of his partners, the United States and the United Kingdom, so that they may jointly decide where they may be better used for the safeguarding and ultimate victory of the united nations. The deciding voice as to the allotment of the goods produced in Canada by Canadian workers and with Canadian materials will remain in the hands of the Canadian government, and rightly so. This makes me more enthusiastic for the vote I shall give, if needed, in favour of this appropriation.
Those are the words I used' in February, and following what I had said I voted and supported and am ready to go on supporting the measure. But in voting to support the government, one should not do it blindly without expressing one's views on different aspects of the questions involved. After all, when a government proposes a policy it is taking as a whole the responsibility for a suggestion of one of its members arising most of the time from advice given by departmental experts. Those experts may be most competent but they are not infallible. They are human beings and they may err. It is therefore perfectly understandable that members of parliament who after all, if we may say so, still represent something and1 are the elected representatives of the people, should when their views are not entirely in accord with those of the experts voice their opinions in the house if their role is to amount to anything.
I for one have the greatest confidence in the judgment of the Prime Minister and I am ready to follow him on this as on most of the other questions that come before the house, but I would consider that I was neglecting my duty if I did not express my personal views and those of my constituents on some of the aspects of this measure.
With the proposal that for the duration of the war we should help and facilitate transactions in order to forward to Britain and our allies the implements of war I am in accord; I approve of it ' entirely. However, our first objective in a Canadian parliament should remain the interest of our own country, Canada. What we have to consider is, can a country like ours afford to do what we are doing any more than Britain can afford to compensate us for our monetary disburse-
Mutual Aid Bill

merits? No matter how good may be my motives to support the measure, to my mind a billion dollar debt will weigh very heavily on the people of Canada, probably more heavily than it would on the people of Britain no matter how much the war may have cost Britain up to this moment. I perfectly understand that Canada should! finance all these charges during the war, but I would expect that we should be compensated in some tangible form so that this further burden imposed upon our people should at least profit us not only in the way of defending our liberties and those of the peoples of the world but also in material compensation.
The ray of hope-and it is upon this that I base my remarks-is contained in paragraph 2 of the resolution which was introduced on May 6 by the Minister of Finance, and which will be found at page 2436 of Hansard, it reads as follows:
That the governor in council may determine the terms and conditions upon which such war supplies are made available to any of the united nations and may require in certain cases payment or repayment in kind or property or reciprocal action or provision of supplies or other direct or indirect benefit as may be deemed appropriate.
This shall be the theme of my remarks just now. What, for instance, is the situation regarding our Canadian securities held in Britain? There has been some talk about it in the press and elsewhere, but we have yet to receive a definite answer as to what is being done so far as the repatriation of these securities is concerned and the kind of repatriation that was done when we did1 repatriate some of them. If we look at the Canadian balance of international payments dated 1939, we find that in the last year for which we had figures at the time and for which we have definite figures now, namely 1937, the debt of Canada held by British citizens or by the British government totalled $2,718,900,000, of which $1,399,200,000 constituted the funded debt of Canada, the provinces and miscellaneous corporations in bonds and debentures.

I have here a report published by the Department of Trade and Commerce, the "Canadian Balance of International Payments," issued this year as to payments in 1941. I see also, according to the report of the Canadian National Railways, that there is quite a difference in the payment of interest on bonds held in private hands, in 1942 and 1941. Unless I am entirely mistaken, it does not in any way improve our financial position. It has helped greatly in the purchase of munitions and supplies for Britain. We have paid these people for their bonds; we have applied the value of these bonds thus repatriated to the purchase of goods for Great Britain, and the Canadian National Railways still owe this amount to the government instead of to British investors. Now this amount, coming out of the funds of our own country, is not the kind of repatriation I would have expected to have been made. I did not think the sum was included in the billion dollars; that is why I looked into the question. Now I see by the report submitted to-day that it is not in the billion dollars, because it is item 7, while the billion dollars is item 12. So that this means a repatriation of moneys above and aside from the billion dollar amount. I am in favour of the billion dollar appropriation; I voted for it. But I am trying to get at the question to see why we should be doing things

of this kind, while Britain has capital and assets which could be transferred and which would benefit our financial position at the end of this war.
The whole control of the common stock and of the majority of the bonds and preferred stock of the Canadian Pacific railway is over there. Some people have said to me, do not propose the repatriation of these securities because it would mean amalgamation. It would of course facilitate facing that situation some day, but it need not be dealt with wholly to the advantage of the Canadian Pacific railway, as some have suggested in the past, but could be handled on terms which would be advantageous to this country. Others say, with regard to the Canadian Pacific railway, that if the government controlled the stock we would be in a bad financial position after the war because even if the economic conditions would bring about a failure of the Canadian Pacific railway, we would have to reimburse the bondholders one hundred cents on the dollar; there would be a repetition of what happened upon the amalgamation of railways under the Canadian National. Of course that might be an objection. On the other hand it can be argued that if the time ever comes when the Canadian Pacific railway cannot face its obligations abroad, the government would have to meet them in order that our credit abroad should be maintained. Therefore I do not think that we would lose much by repatriation, because in any event, if Canadian Pacific railway bonds were in default, the same people who to-day object to my proposal would say that we had to compensate people abroad whose investments were affected in order to maintain the credit and good name of the country. Furthermore, if we had the securities we would be in a position, if we wanted to do so, to dictate the terms when it comes to merge the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian National railway.
Some people seem scandalized because, although I approve the grant, I talk of practical money questions. I think it is our duty to do so. Take, for example, the present situation of Montreal. The people of that city will have to pay more in taxation connected1 with these two billions of dollars than the value involved in recent negotiations between Montreal and the financiers of London about the municipal debt which was floated in England. These negotiations have been going on for a long time, and as I say, the citizens of Montreal will pay more in the taxation involved in these two billion dollars than the amount represented by the suggested plan of refund for their municipal bonds. We might ask that

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
I followed with a good deal of interest the remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. I cannot agree with his peroration when he indicates that in time of war, when our defence is at stake in all parts of the world, commercial considerations should be before us. I rise to say a few words this afternoon because of some of the provisions of this bill which for the most part have not yet been referred to, although in his concluding remarks the hon. gentleman did refer to one of them.
I think the minister has not given us a full and complete explanation of this bill. An examination of its provisions leads me to believe that it is an epoch-making measure, one of the most important that has come before this parliament, and its implications are such that they become apparent only after careful scrutiny and examination of the various sections.
In its inception this bill is an application of the principles of the lend-lease legislation in effect, in the United States, and the mutual aid legislation in effect in some other countries. Lend-lease is the foundation principle of this bill. As to the principles of mutual aid no one can have any difference of view. Mutual aid among the allied1 and united1 nations had its part in the victories won in the last few days in Tunisia and North Africa. This bill is an adoption and adaptation of the lend-lease legislation. In order to arrive at a conclusion as to what this bill actually means other than the provisions for defence it becomes necessary to consider the lend-lease

Mutual Aid Bill
legislation of the United States and the comments that have been made thereon by the President of the United States and other officials.
The bill has three phases or aspects. First is the phase of national and international defence. The second has to do with the integration of production amongst the various nations. The third, and to me the most important phase requiring elucidation, is the part relating to post-war rehabilitation in the international sphere.
So far as contribution to the united nations is concerned I give to this bill absolute and unqualified support. It is but a continuation of the legislation of last year under which Canada, in assisting Britain by the billion dollar vote, was in fact assisting herself. The legislation of last year showed empire solidarity. This legislation, in so far as it consists of a defence contribution of $1,000,000,000 to the united nations, shows the solidarity of the united nations. It shows also that the people of Canada realize that this is a people's war; that it is not a national or British empire war but a war of all the peoples within the united nations, the contribution of each to be measured by the fact that all we have shall be placed in the common pool for victory. It shows that we are in partnership with the freedom-loving nations and that to this partnership we will give our all. It means in effect that to-day Canada recognizes that this war is world^wide in scope; that we in common with the other united nations must mobilize our efforts on the same front line and the same production line; that by cooperation among the united nations there will be strength; that through collaboration there will be power; that through the mutual distribution of goods and services an irresistible wall of offence and defence will be built up within the united nations, and that this mutual contribution on the part of the nations within the empire and the united nations is the result of a grand strategy to prevent jealousies and economic difficulties arising after the war.
The extension of lend-lease, which started in the United States as assistance for Great Britain, to include the other united nations, came as a result of negotiation with the various countries, and it is interesting to note that in framing this legislation, in many particulars, consciously or unconsciously the actual words of the lend-lease legislation in the United States have been used. I am going to refer in particular to article 7 of the lend-lease legislation in the United States, which contains words very like those used in
72537-162J	[DOT]
the preamble of the bill now before the committee. It provides that the terms and conditions of that settlement-
. . . shall he such as not to burden commerce between the two countries-
It started off as between Britain and the United States.
-but to promote mutually advantageous economic relations between (the signatories) and the betterment of world wide economic relations. To that end, they shall include provision for agreed action by the United States of America and the United Kingdom, open to participation by all other countries of like mind-
I take it that now Canada comes within the ambit of those words, "countries of like mind."
-directed to the expansion, by appropriate international and domestic measure, of production, employment and the exchange and consumption of goods, which are the material foundations of the liberty and welfare of all the citizens;-
Then it goes on to say:
-to the elimination of all forms of discriminatory treatment in international commerce, and to the reduction of tariffs and other trade barriers; and in general, to the attainment of all the economic objectives set forth in the joint declaration made on August 12, 1941, by the President of the United States of America and the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.
In other words the Atlantic charter.
A't an early convenient date, conversations shall be begun between the two governments with a view to determining, in the light of governing economic conditions, the best means of attaining the above stated objectives by their own agreed action and of seeking the agreed action of other like-minded governments.
I pause here to point out that as yet parliament and this country have not received any information from the minister as to whether there has been any collaboration between Canada, Great Britain and the United States in reference to a plan for after the war, within the framework of the lend-lease system. At this point the following questions occur to me, and I should like the minister to answer them in due course. Is this bill part of a general scheme among the united nations for the attainment of the objectives named in article 7? If so, will the minister produce the correspondence and give the house a record of the negotiations that have taken place in order to achieve these purposes? I pause here to say this. If this bill went no further than to provide for aid to the united nations to the extent of $1,000,000,000, these questions would not arise; but this bill, in its import and in its terms, lays the foundation for a commercial organization among the united nations after the war. In
Mutual Aid Bill

the allocation of foodstuffs and munitions and supplies, will there be a central director among the united nations who will determine the nature of the contribution to be made by each nation? Is Canada's contribution to be allocated by a central board of direction, or is Canada's contribution to be haphazard, dependent only upon the decision of the members of the cabinet comprising the committee? Will it be distributed after consultation with the other united nations?
At this point let me say that I cannot understand why Canada, occupying an increasingly important position in the national and international world, does not have representation on all the major boards that operate in Washington. Why have we no representation on the food board? Just in that connection, next week we are sending representatives of Canada to attend a food conference in the United States, but they are not to be accompanied by a minister of the crown. At that conference the future of agriculture and food production may well be determined, yet not a member of this House of Commons knows what powers these men possess; not a 'member knows what they are going to do when they get there, or has any conception of the course or policy that is to be followed by them.
The second aspect in connection with lend-lease and mutual aid is in the scheme for the integration of production, something that has not been dealt with as yet by the Minister of Munitions and Supply. It was dealt with in part the otheT day by the Minister of Finance, who used these words at page 2439 of Hansard:
This system of Mutual Aid will enable our great productive power, industrial and agricultural, to be most fully and effectively used in the prosecution of the war. It will enable us to exert a balanced effort in accordance with the nature of our own resources-the type of effort that we are best able to make quickly and effectively.
Then a little further down:
The products of our factories, of our mines and forests and refineries, should go where they are most immediately effective in winning the war. . . .
There is reference there to the question of the integration of the industrial production of this and the other united nations in such a way as to maximize the power of the united nations.
I turn now to the attitude of the United States of America on this question in an effort to ascertain exactly what their attitude is. The purpose of the extension of the lend-lease act and the creation of the committees that have been set up in Washington is to secure an intregation of production to the
end that each of the united nations will produce those commodities or munitions which it is peculiarly able to do. I ask this: What is Canada's production to be in this great productive effort, in this mobilization of the resources of the united nations? What is Canada's plan to be?
Have we arrived yet at the place where the government can say to the people of Canada-I think the time has come having regard to the catastrophic position in which man-power in Canada now is-this will be our contribution; we will contribute so many men to the armed forces, so many to munitions production and so many to agriculture. In debating the principles of lend-lease by Canada to the other united nations and the integration of the production of the united nations, we in this parliament should receive from the government the plan or the blueprint-there must be some blueprint-of our production. This must be done if we are to integrate our production with that of the other united nations. I ask the minister if negotiations are now under way to the end that Canada shall produce only certain materials or munitions of war? What is the plan in so far as Canada is concerned?
Within the last few weeks there has been a change in the war-time production of Canada. I am not going to deal with this phase at the moment, but we all know that there has been a suggestion that there is to be a reduction in tank production and that Canada is to devote far more of her productive capacity to the production of ships. Now, as to the production of aeroplanes, I refer to Lancasters in particular, my information is that after months of tooling and preparation in one great factory in this country, there was suddenly a discontinuance of production without any explanation. Was that on account of the fact that a new plan has been evolved among the united nations, whereby Canada's production will be limited to production of .those things most needed and producible in Canada such as agricultural products, certain munitions and shipping?
What opportunity is Canada to have under this scheme to dispose of her agricultural products? As I read the debates and the reports issued by the United States government, that country has gradually arrived at the point whereby agricultural products make up only 3 per cent of what is advanced under lend-lease. Is Canada under this system to devote herself more and more to agricultural production? If that is the scheme, we should be told. When Canada is prepared to contribute a billion dollars to the united

Mutual Aid Bill
nations, is it not proper that in the purchase of agricultural products for transshipment to the united nations under this bill the farmer should receive a fair and proper parity price?
That is the picture we have in so far as integration is concerned. Never have we in this house, within the last year or at any other time, been given a picture of what the plan is, how our man-power is to be distributed and just what Canada's contribution will be. In this connection I should like to read what the President of the United States said in the report he mpde to congress some three months after March 11, 1942. He said:
The programme of lend-lease arrangements is also emerging as a factor in the combined effort of the united nations to weave a pattern for peace. Those agreements are taking shape as key instruments of national policy, the first of our concrete steps in the direction of affirmative post-war reconstruction.
At no time has the minister in explaining this legislation indicated that it forms a basis, such as was suggested by the President of the United States, of post-war reconstruction. It is to this phase of the bill that I intend to direct considerable attention. The President continued:
We are now in the war, as we were not in March, 1941, when the lend-lease act was passed. We have pledged our resources without limit to win the war and the peace which will follow it. We look forward to a period of security and liberty, in which men may freely pursue lives of their choice, and governments will achieve policies leading to full and useful production and employment. If the promise of the peace is to be fulfilled, a large volume of production and trade among nations must be restored and sustained. This trade must be solidly founded on stable exchange relationships and liberal principles of commerce. The lend-lease settlement will rest on the specific and detailed programme for achieving these ends which are, as article 7 of the agreements with Great Britain, China and Russia points out, "the material foundations of the liberty and welfare of all peoples."
This is the significant portion of the President's statement:
Cooperative action among the united nations is contemplated to fulfil this programme for economic progress, in the many spheres where action is needed. It is hoped that plans will soon develop for a series of agreements and recommendations for legislation, in the fields of commercial policy, of money and finance, international investment and reconstruction. . . . We have affirmatively declared our intention to avoid the political and economic mistakes of international debt experience during the twenties. A lend-lease settlement which fulfils this principle will be sound from the economic point of view. But it will have a greater merit. It will represent the only fair way to distribute the financial costs of war among the united nations.
Then Mr. Sumner Welles in a speech referring to the significance of agreements and mutual aid schemes, such as the present one, said that the master lend-lease agreement is the first important milestone on the road to the achievement of the objective set forth in the Atlantic charter. The report to congress contains words to the effect that "the form and terms of this agreement represent the culmination of many months of study and negotiation, and the solution they foreshadow promises to contribute substantially to the post-war reconstruction in which the United States has so large a political and economic stake."
I ask the minister to tell us the post-war plans that are contemplated under Bill No. 76. What decisions have been arrived at by the government? What deliberations have taken place in order to- bring into a unity of purpose and aim the various united nations? This bill has been designed as a means of assistance through national and international contribution to the united nations, and with that aim and principle I agree. But there are so many terms in this bill that go beyond the matter of contribution and assistance that one wonders why they should ever have been included, in the bill unless it was intended that it should operate as an abdication by parliament of its right to control the making of commercial treaties and arrangements both now and after the war. Mr. Sumner Welles has pointed out that the united nations have agreed that the principles of lend-lease shall be the basis upon which the post-war reconstruction of the worldi shall take place, and "will be a cooperative mechanism not only for war but for peace and reconstruction.." He indicated that for a period of from three to four or five or six years after hostilities end there might be no- peace treaty made until reconstruction has taken place among the nations of the world, and that during that period of time the principles and policies of lend-lease might well be carried into effect in all parts of the world. I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that you appreciate the significance of this matter. It means that if parliament passes this bill in its present form, it turns over to the members of the cabinet who are on this Mutual Aid committee the right to determine the commercial policy of this nation with others of the united nations and with other nations outside the united nations not only until the conclusion, of the war but until the conclusion of the peace treaty.
Let us look at the terms of this bill. If the bill does not mean what I suggest, that sliows how dangerous it is in drafting a bill to copy
Mutual Aid Bill

the terms of some other legislation, which carries with it the significance I am now attaching to this. Let me read the preamble of the bill. It states:
. . . and whereas it is essential to the defence and security of Canada and to the cause of world freedom that Canada should make the utmost contribution to the victory of the united nations; . . . and whereas it is expedient that the conditions upon which Canadian war supplies are made available to other united nations should not be such as to burden post-war commerce or lead to the imposition of trade restrictions or otherwise prejudice a just and enduring peace.
The united nations are defined as those nations which were signatories to the agreement whereby the expression "united nations" came into being. But the -bill not only includes them; it permits the governor in council to designate any other nation or authority which has been associated with Canada in the prosecution of the war. Is that supposed to cover the ambit of lend-lease in the United States where the President has the power to give assistance not only to nations within the united nations but to others believed to be of assistance?
Then I turn to section 3 which provides for the determination of the distribution of war supplies under this bill. Section 3 reads:
There shall be a board to be called the Canadian Mutual Aid Board consisting of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Justice . . . which shall be charged with the administration of this act.
It was the hon. gentleman who just took his seat who put his finger on this clause which is the most dangerous of all in the matter of parliament relinquishing its power to require the government to submitting trade agreements to this house. Section 4 reads:
The board may on behalf of His Majesty, in accordance with the strategic needs of the war, contribute . . . and make available war supplies to any of the united nations.
Then subsection 2 of section 4 continues:
It shall be good and sufficient consideration for making war supplies available to any of the united nations hereunder that the said war supplies are to be used in the joint and effective prosecution of the war

My submission is that no other principle should apply, and that these supplies should be made available only upon the strategic ground of common defence Whereby contributions are made to a common pool of supplies for common defence. But this same subsection goes on to say:
-but no war supplies shall be so made available to any of the united nations except upon terms and conditions approved by the governor in council or by regulations, and the governor

in council may require, in respect of specific classes of supplies or any specific transfer of supplies under subsection one of this section, such payment or repayment in kind or property or such reciprocal action or provision of supplies-
Then here -comes the significant part:

or such other direct or indirect benefit as the governor in council deems appropriate.
That provision in my opinion takes this bill outside the ambit of qualification depending upon the necessities of war and exigencies of strategy, and places in the hands of the governor in council the power to enter into trade arrangements and trade relations which may remain effective not only throughout the war but until the signing of the peace treaty. In other words, by the addition of those words parliament hands over to the governor in council the right to determine what trade relations shall be entered into as a quid pro quo for the contribution and assistance given hereunder by Canada. If it is otherwise, why not end the sentence in this way: Good and sufficient consideration for making war supplies under this bill, and the only consideration for making war supplies available to any of the united nations, is that the war supplies are to be used in the joint effective prosecution of the war? Why add a provision that enables the governor in council, on the recommendation of members of this cabinet, to say to any nation within the united nations: You shall receive assistance from us if in return you give to us some trade consideration either now or after the war? If parliament passes this bill as it now stands, parliament is giving the power to the governor in council, upon the recommendation of this Mutual Aid board, to enter into any trade relations which may bind Canada both now and after the war, and parliament will have abdicated her right to have brought before it any agreements so entered into.
Why, the bill even goes so far in section 8 which to my mind is the most astounding section of the whole bill that it provides -that:
As soon as practicable after the close of each fiscal year, the board shall prepare and lay before parliament a report of operations under this act except such information as the governor in council deems it incompatible with the public interest to disclose.
The governor in council, the members of the cabinet, exercise that right every day in this house now. When we ask questions from this side of the house, how often we are told that it is not compatible with the public interest to disclose the information. We have resisted that course, but now we are asked to place upon the statute books of this country the right, which the government already possesses, of denying information to members of this

Mutual Aid Bill
parliament. What are its implications? The governor in council could enter into a reciprocal agreement with any one of the united nations in return for support and assistance under this bill; and if we were to ask for information as to what agreements had been entered into, whether any reciprocal transactions had been arrived at, or what decisions had been made, the doors would be closed by ourselves having placed parliamentary approval in advance of the circumstances arising. As I understand this clause, parliament is to tie its own hands, to shackle itself by depriving itself of the right to receive information to which it is entitled. Hon. members, when they were met with the answer, "It is not in the public interest", have invariably realized that the responsibility for the decision whether the disclosure of a matter is or is not contrary to the public interest, rests with the government. To-day we are asked by legislation to show that we have gone far along the road to the denial of our rights as members to obtain information. Section 8 means that the governor in council can enter into agreements which will bind governments after the war is over. The bill specifically empowers the governor in council to enter into any agreements and any relations whatsoever binding parliament after this war. Parliament might well be in the position of not knowing what arrangements have been entered into, what tariff decisions or conclusions have been arrived at.
I ask the minister to make changes in this bill. No one objects to the power conferred on this board to give assistance to all or any of the united nations. We on this side have always stood for that principle. Often we have been ridiculed because we believed in an ever-widening war effort. We support this bill unreservedly in so far as it makes effective the determination of parliament to uphold and aid the power of the united nations. Speaking for myself, I say that I object to parliament abdicating its right to have placed before it treaties, agreements or transactions, other than on strategical matters, in connection with the operation of this measure. I ask the minister to make alterations in the bill to provide that if trade treaties or other commercial arrangements are entered into, they shall not be effective until they have been approved by parliament; they shall be effective only in so far as they consist of the granting of assistance for military defence-that power we have to hand over to the government-but they shall not be effective to bind the people of this country, its industry and its labour, without parliament first having an opportunity of passing thereon.
I believe this is the first time that legislation has been brought before this parliament so contrary to the principles of parliamentary government. Even before Pearl Harbor, when the United States was neutral excepting that she knew who her friends were, her lend-lease measure contained- no such provisions. To-day it contains no such provisions.

Mutual Aid Bill

The President from time to time, but not less frequently than once every ninety days-
The time is shorter there.

I understood my hon. friend to say there was nothing like that in the United States act. Well, I have read the portion of the United States act from which these words were taken; and for some reason or another the congress of the United States does not seem to have been outraged by the suggestion that strategic considerations in the time of a bitter wrar would make it necessary for certain information not to be placed on the record. That was the reason, and the only reason why these words were inserted. It is of the utmost importance that we do not at times give certain information about certain assistance which is extended to our allies. To give that information would help our enemies. Anybody who knows anything about it knows that, and for that reason we cannot put in the statute a direction to the government, to give all the information about what we are doing along certain lines. We cannot do it, and we have to insert a guarding clause. This idea, that it was put in to prevent us from telling the house about some sinister commercial trade agreements that we might enter into with various nations of the world, is a figment of the imagination. It is so far-fetched that it is hardly worthy of serious consideration in this house.
My hon. friend says that under an earlier clause of the agreement we have power to enter into trade arrangements, and he wishes to make it clear that parliament will have the right to reject any trade advantages that we might get. That is what it comes to-that there must be power of rejection of trade advantages. Certainly I did not have any intention of entering into trade agreements under this clause. It might be that it would be possible to get some trade advantage, but certainly we are not approaching this whole problem in that spirit. What we had in mind was mainly in regard to certain equipment that would be of value after the war, certain goods that might be of value after the war, perhaps merchant ships which it might reasonably be stipulated' would be returned to us if of value; and I do not think there would be anything wrong about

that. There would be nothing harsh, unreasonable or niggardly about such an attitude. But one cannot foresee all the reasonable requests of that kind which it might be desirable to make, and that is the reason for the somewhat general language of the section. speechtext:
I believe it is generally regarded as a gentleman's agreement. At least, that is what I have always understood in the years I have been here. If anyone in this country, however important his position in the public administration, had dared to ask during the first year of the war that Canada lend a billion dollars to the mother country, our
72.537-163
budget being a little over 8500,000,000, he would have been described as insane. If during the second year of the war, our budget having doubled, the same man had dared to ask the country for a second billion, we would perhaps have considered him as a public enemy. If the same man had said in ' 1939 that the country's budget would have doubled during the fourth year-and Canada's debt was two billions in 1920-that man would have been branded with some new unenviable qualification. Nevertheless, such is our country's posi-' tion now, and no sign is visible that gives us any hope for a stop in this whirlwind race. This second billion dollars is going through the different stages of parliamentary procedure without meeting with that numerical opposition which one would expect from the representatives of a country with a population of twelve million. We are far from that free, voluntary and moderate effort which was promised us at the beginning of this war by a party in its first act of treachery. Forgetting, or pretending to forget its anti-participation promises and nationalistic sermons doled out to us during a period of twenty years, this party was putting into operation the most accurately and cleverly organized propaganda in order to prepare public opinion in Canada little by little and bring it around to accept willingly or by coercion the most exhausting war effort ever imposed on any country. I said by coercion because, if coercion was not applied as crudely as in 1917-18, nevertheless it exists. By means of different small pressures a whole population, practically against its will, is brought to admit, almost as an accomplished fact, what yesterday was looked upon even by its masters as an impossibility. As a matter of fact, our men are forced to volunteer for overseas service.
In order that there be a free effort, a minimum of existing liberty is necessary, including the radical power to choose. Were we not allowed to choose between neutrality and participation? Hansard shows quite clearly that when a group of hon. members spoke of neutrality our important statesmen were greatly scandalized. If the terms applied to those who now dare to make use of their right to discuss had been invented four years ago, this belittling that is so often practised against us on the radio and at public meetings by those who are badly in need of the people's forgiveness would be four years older. Ireland could remain and has remained neutral, but Canada several thousand miles distant from the conflict, was not given this liberty.

Mutual Aid Bill

A declaration of war was made en vitesse, without a vote-Hansard registers "on division"-in spite of the pressing demand of the late chief of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, Mr. Woodsworth. The next day participation was announced by the demand for a subsidy of 8100,000,000. Those who wanted to oppose participation- there were sixteen of them-had to move three different, separate motions (two of which, those moved by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie and the hon. member for Montiporency, were ruled out of order) to get a vote in committee. Parliament had decided and was ruled by the manufacturers of promises against participation. But honour was safe; parliament had decided.
Having entered the conflict, Canada was no longer free to choose between neutrality and participation. She could not possibly withdraw from that conflict in which the avowed imperialists had deeply engaged her.
The second meaning of liberty lying in the exercise of this power to choose, the position thereby accorded us made it solid and identical with the first.
The third meaning of liberty is the state in which an intelligent and free being exists and where those who surround him facilitate the exercise of his will, or at least do not erect any barriers to it. The history of the present war in Canada proved beyond doubt that the governmental, imperialist and financial propaganda not only did not facilitate the exercise of this right but hindered its manifestation down to the smallest details. We are no more free to choose between giving or refusing this second gift of one thousand million dollars. At least morally speaking we are not free to choose.
The plebiscite demonstrated that only those who favoured the "yes" were accorded the right to use the Canadian broadcasting system, our national system financed by public funds. Those who favoured the "no" had to be content with the private stations, and this small group of ours had to multiply itself to cover the territory in the limited time allotted them. It is the just right of our group to make use of the national network, and it will claim this right as long as this complete liberty, on which our country is supposed to have a claim, as a result of its gifts of billions and an exaggerated participation, is not accorded it on the same footing as other existing parties.

We claimed it several
times and we will continue to do so. We are far from having a Hyde park or an Albert

hall in Canada. Most of our speeches in public meetings are carefully followed and sometimes reported in) shorthand. There must be a master in psychology among the members of the present government. He must also be a master of political history and excel in the manipulation of public opinion, on the one hand relying on excessive imperialism, which has always been foremost in the minds of a certain number of so-called Canadians, for whom Canadian soil is but a particle of the motherland, and on the other hand relying on the belief of a part of the population in those men whose reputation as autonomists and real Canadians helped to hide for many years this real, deep-rooted colonial spirit, awaiting the proper time for a sure birth and change to an exaggerated imperialism.
One cannot change in one night the mentality of a whole population. One cannot erase from the mind of a whole province the memory of a promise, reiterated a thousand times, not only that never again would conscription be imposed for overseas service, but even that her armies would never again participate in any external war. In 1917 the Liberals, during a political campaign, heaped upon the then Conservative conscriptionists the sourest reproaches. If at that time any man had dared to speak of a gift to England not of 835,000,000 but of $500,000,000, he would have had to face a crowd readiy to* stone him. Nevertheless these same Liberals or their political descendants to-day try to put us under the ban of public opinion; although our only wrongdoing is to continue to preach the doctrine of which they professed themselves the convinced apostles. Strange to say, during the last forty-five years our soldiers have seen fighting in different theatres of war, having been three times called and sent beyond' the limits of Canadian soil. Two of these occasions, the South African war and the second world war, were under a Liberal government and the other under a Conservative government. Even then, a certain number of Liberals were united for conscription; a fine record for anti-participa-tionists and amti-conscriptionists!

speechtext:
I am just coming to it, Mr. Chairman; I have to make a little explanation first. I am speaking of the billion dollars and of those who promised to

Mutual Aid Bill
keep away from external wars. Now that they find1 themselves at the limit of our Canadian effort, not only do they ask us to go ahead, but they ask us to give a billion dollars, and soon they will ask us to give half a dozen billions. That is what I am trying to prove. We are far from the promises we were given in 1939 and 1940, of a moderate, voluntary war effort. Now we are giving billions, so that I think I am absolutely in order in coming to that gift of a billion dollars after having explained' what the Liberal party has done before.
Circumstances came to the help of these champions, and the first military budgets- not for a billion-were voted in this house in 1937-38, framed by protestations of loyalty to promises and categorical declarations during three by-elections, in Bonaventure, Lot-biniere and St. Henri. Then war broke out, and the great master of history and psychology of the cabinet must have scrutinized the political history of Europe and, in particular, English imperialism, whose diplomatic ability had reached its apogee during the period 1903 to 1914. France had not as yet forgotten the Dreyfus case and the unlucky adventure of Fashoda. The third republic, which was imposed upon France by powers from without, did not succeed in making the French people forget a century and a half of strife. We are on the billion dollar gift, but the billion dollars cannot make us forget the years of nationalist preaching, and I have to explain that. Only eleven years of neighbourly intercourse was necessary to have France accept the war of 1914 as a revenge and a recovery of territorial possessions. France won the last war, but notwithstanding her enormous sacrifices she found herself cut off from the indemnity due by the aggressor. That is the truth; she was cut off by a series of intrigues, pacts, understandings and treaties which she had to accept. I have read the history of the year 1922, and I know what I am saying now is the exact truth.
In Canada, all that the master psychologist had to do was make the people forget twenty years of anti-participation and anti-conscription, preachings. It was not found necessary to multiply the testimonials of affection to have parliament decide to declare war. A well organized propaganda and a single but far-famed phrase were all that were necessary: "We freely declare war and will fight side by side with England and her allies. The effort will be free, voluntary and moderate." That was the phrase; but in giving this billion we are not fighting side by side; we are going ahead of England.
72537-163*
No other country is making the effort Canada is now making, and the truth of that statement is shown in the recent, budgets of several nations. The old anti-conscription war-horse remained [DOT] in the race, and the federal election of 1940 saw him nose in first, leaving behind promises, words of honour, oaths and so on. It was then, I believe, that the country witnessed the handshake of the two old parties. One continued its propaganda of total war effort; the other feigned to give in to the first, though not without regrets; taking good care, however, not to offend the susceptibilities of a large portion of the Canadian people who had been their pillar and strength during at least a decade.
During the course of the debate on military credits in 1937, amidst the muffled laughter of statesmen to be, and protests of fidelity to sworn promises, we said, "A country of ten million men, caught up by the fever of war and by imperial enthusiasm, raised a considerable army in a few months. Public men categorically opposed to participation in external wars voted the sending of troops to help out the empire." The same men, who were opposed to any participation twenty years ago, now want another billion. "These sacrifices were made by an unprepared country. The vote we are being asked to cast on the increased military credits is a vote that will increase our defence capacity but also our capacity to contribute when the tocsin sounds. If history should repeat itself and emergencies become stronger than the will of the leading men, there will no longer be time to oppose armaments and manifest our desire to be nonpartisans in any external war in which the empire might be interested." We said that in 1937, to warn the government not to go to war and not to go too fast. I have to explain that if the government had listened carefully and paid attention to what we said, we would not be so deeply involved now in an exaggerated war effort. I have to explain this, Mr. Chairman, in order to show the committee that we have a right and we, are entitled to speak against this measure providing for a second gift of a billion dollars. We went on to say at that time, "How much more alluring it will be for the lords of the admiralty, helped by circumstances and events"-we should 'have added, helped by a wisely organized propaganda-"to force Canadian sentiment whenever the country may be ready to assume a contribution more adequate to its means."
We were called faint-hearted men; in certain quarters, not openly but behind the curtain,

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when
the committee rose at six o'clock I was getting closer and closer to a discussion of this gift of one billion dollars, the second gift we have presented to England and our allies. Some say, in the province of Quebec especially, that we are always opposed to conscription, but our soldiers are to be found in the West Indies, Newfoundland and other countries, including Alaska. A few billions are handed out here and there, but there still remains that order in council which gives a one-way fare straight to England. It is said that we must not defeat the present government, because, it is asked, where could we find men to replace it?
Even history is distorted in order to accuse us of having voted against the national defence credits. Someone, through what I would deem to be ignorance, has gone further and said on the radio that not one member of our group has voted against participation. We will let Hansard refute these false accusations. We will say to those in the province of Quebec who say that the French Canadians ought to do more than the others that we do not intend to ask forgiveness for having been born French Canadians. Those who excel in zealousness must realize that zealousness is next to subservience. To those who speak on the radio and pretend that we harm French-Canadian groups in. other provinces we say that we cannot understand this reproach for -wanting to make free use of our rights when they themselves have struggled for the recognition of the same rights and the maintenance of their schools, their language and their faith. It is the Quebec nationalists who came to their help and who will do it

again notwithstanding the reproaches which have been offered. The argument against having too many political parties in this country falls flat when we consider that the victorious France of 1914 had at least eight different parties. The reason why they exist in Canada is the failure of the old parties to find a real, thorough and sincere Canadian policy.
It is no longer a matter of thinking of Canada first, of minding our own business and of letting European countries settle their own quarrels. While the present government tries to make the public believe by a national security and reconstruction programme that it intends to take care of Canadian problems after the war, we hear other propaganda in favour of mass immigration which would only add to our domestic problems. It is then that we will need our billions which, have been given away to prevent the long heart-rending bread-lines which were to be found during the last unemployment crisis.
The first war costs us over $50,000,000 in pensions. It is only fair that the wounded and the sick soldiers who return should be properly treated, and this will mean that an equal amount, if not a greater amount, will be needed' after this war. These gifts would be welcomed then if they had been controlled before. What are we doing to prepare ourselves to face a possible epidemic similar to that of 1918? Every war brings an epidemic which spreads as fast as the wind through the remotest countries. What is being done to meet this eventuality? We shall need the billions we are giving away now to carry on public works which would help to remedy the crisis that inevitably follows all wars. Shall we again be answered, with the statement that there is no money except to provide a dole for the unemployed? Shall we again open up concentration camps where men will be paid twenty cents a day as a palliative?
Two. of the most perplexing problems that will occur after the war will be in connection with agriculture and labour. It is a known fact that work in factories or army life diverts men from agriculture. Shall we be able to offer anything but a disorganized agriculture to our returned men who were born farmers or farmers' sons? Shall we be in a position to offer the labourer but a foot when the cannon merchants decide to take a holiday and when there is no employment to be found in the non-essential industries which will have been disorganized? Some one will say that I am a defeatist, a saboteur of the war effort. Little care we about such state-

Mutual Aid Bill
ments. We. have learned to' think as Canadians, to see the interests of Canada before the interests of other countries.

If other nations have their problems, so have we. If we are to face them, it must not be with disorganized public works, with a destroyed economy or with an anaemic population whose courage is gone. It is all right to give billions, but some day we shall have to pay. Others have suffered and died to find out that gratefulness exists among the masses, but the .petty interests of the profiteers will erase all gratitude.
Some say that it is but the surplus of our production that we give. If we have a surplus of production,, let us give back to the farm those hands which are lacking and which are necessary to produce the food needed by our people. Perhaps we do not suffer rationing to the same extent as the nations directly in the conflict, but with the expanse of tillable land we have in Canada there is no reason why the labourer who toils night and day in. a more or less sanitary factory should be rationed. There is no ' reason why we should ration the farmer who grows his own food, and there is still less reason why we should ration, the sanatoriums and the hospitals which care for a large portion of our population, and the educational institutions which have the care of growing children. Some of these establishments will have to close their doors and send back to their families the sick, the infirm and even the patients with contagious diseases. Wonderful results in a country that hands out money by the billion!
Just now thousands of families are unable to find suitable lodgings, and others have to put up with miserable huts. A marvellous situation for a country which could use its surplus of production to benefit its own people but which prefers to give it to others! Imperial enthusiasm and war fever are the two spiritual ailments which have been suffered by our leaders since 1939. Let us hope that these
things will soon disappear in the face of the bare realities which wall be imposed, by force of circumstances and by the awakening of the people, upon those from whom so much has been expected and by whom we have been so pitifully deceived.
Air. LaCROIX (Quebec-Montmorency): May I make a suggestion to the Minister of Finance? Why does he not include in this bill a clause which will enable this government, through the British government, to bring back to Canada all Canadian securities now in the hands of the English people? I am mentioning that fact, not because I am in favour of merging the Canadian National railways with the Canadian Pacific railway, but because necessities after the war may force the government to act. The railway surplus is no doubt good at the present time, but conditions will change after the war, so why not include in the bill now a clause which will force the return through the British government of our Canadian railway securities now in the hands of the British people. It is no secret that the majority of the shares of the Canadian Pacific Railway company are in the hands of British shareholders, and if we had such a clause in the bill we could take advantage of it to protect ourselves in case the amalgamation of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific became a necessity later on. I make that suggestion.
