speechtext: The answer is that we do not regard the contribution we are to make under this bill as a sale to Great Britain. We regard it as our contribution to a common cause. That is the fundamental difference, I presume, between the hon. gentlemen on the one side and myself and the government on the other. If this were to be regarded as a commercial transaction, that what we contribute to this war from now on be regarded as a sale to Great Britain, then we ought to get paid for it; but if it is regarded as a contribution to the common cause, we should not. That is the simplest way in which I can answer my hon. friend.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
This bill does not provide for a gift to Great Britain. It is specifically stated by the minister that this is a contribution to the common cause.
The hon. member for Lake Centre this afternoon made an analytical and what I considered to be a very constructive speech. The minister on the spur of the moment sought to disparage the suggestions made by the hon. gentleman, who had no doubt given careful study to the interpretation of certain sections of this bill, or particularly sections 4 and 8. I
Mutual Aid Bill

suggest to the minister that he do not lightly discard the logic of the hon. member for Lake Centre, but that he review his suggestions in the calm light of moderate reflection, and then I think he will agree-I am trying to be as moderate as I can-that there is room for the interpretation which the hon. member for Lake Centre placed upon certain of these sections, having regard to the background which he established. Therefore I am suggesting to the minister that he might very well consider a revision of the language used in the draftsmanship of this bill.
There cannot, I think, be very much objection to subsection 1 of section 4, but in the view of some of us the implications contained in all that part of subsection 2 which follows after the word "war" in line 45 are such that the government might conceivably do what the hon. member for Lake Centre indicated in his view they could do under the authority contained in the latter part of that subsection. But the minister immediately reacted to that suggestion adversely, and he gave it as a statement of fact that the government never had any such intention as was suggested might arise out of the operation of that section. I want to give the minister credit for being absolutely honest and sincere when he made that statement., but I say to him frankly that on a first reading of this bill I was a bit uneasy about that section. I thought the powers contained in it were exceedingly wide, and I still think they are very wide. They are powers that the government should not ask parliament even in war time to give them. Therefore I would suggest to the minister that he review the latter part of subsection 2 of section) 4 in the light of the observations which have fallen from the lips of the hon. member for Lake Centre.
I have not made any study of the bases of this legislation, such as the United States lend-lease bill, but I can understand that on a liberal construction and interpretation of this section it is capable of the implications suggested by the hon. member for Lake Centre. If that is not in the minister's mind, and I take it for granted from what he told us before the dinner recess that no such intention exists as to enter into negotiations with any of the allied nations in connection with the giving of war supplies whereby they would be bound to make reciprocal arrangements which in the days to come might carry over through the post-war period and create a situation which parliament itself never contemplated and would not have sanctioned if it had contemplated it, then I suggest that he ought to restrict the application of section 4. That is the suggestion I make to him. Indeed, he

could in my view very well end subsection 2 at the word "war" in line 45; but if he is insistent that certain powers should be conferred upon the executive with respect to terms and conditions, then the section might read something like this: that the supplies , are to be used in the joint and effective prosecution of the war upon such terms and conditions in respect of those supplies as the governor in council may impose with respect, we will say, to the return at a subsequent period of supplies not used or with respect to a contribution in kind or of some: other nature, or w-ith respect to sending us supplies which an allied nation might have available for use by" us during the war period. But as it is now, there is no doubt that upon a wide interpretation of the section the government could do almost anything it wished. Therefore I suggest to the minister that if there must be limitations, they should be specific limitations rather than couched in terms of such a wide and general character.
That suggestion is offered in a friendly spirit. I have a simple mind, and I did not read into the sections of this statute suggestions which have since arisen, but I had a vague, intuitive, uneasy feeling that the government were, perhaps, taking undue powers, and that there was not, we will say, with all charity, full and frank disclosure. Perhaps I should not go even that far, because I supported this bill on a statement of the Minister of Finance and on a supplementary statement of the Minister of Munitions and Supply with respect to the question of operating under the statute; and unquestionably I approve what the government is primarily seeking to do, namely, to make a contribution, not a sale, based on the theory" that we all are part and parcel in a common cause and our contribution should be to the common cause; that Canada can do it, and that we should not look upon this as a matter in which we should exact a quid pro quo from anybody. Heaven knows, any contribution which Canada makes to Britain has been amply paid, and was amply' paid in 1939, 1940, 1941, and down to the very day in 1943 when the battle of Tunisia was won. It has been paid not only by the fighting men of the British army, but by the magnificent bravery and achievements of the British navy and British airmen, reinforced by" the Canadian navy and by the noble band of young men whom we have sent overseas to join their forces to defend Canada and to keep this war away from our shores.
There is one other observation I wish to make with respect to section 8.

I submit that, on section 1 of a bill, when one has not spoken on the second reading, it is open to, and advantage has been taken of the opportunity this afternoon by many hon. members, to make some general observations. I wish to make a constructive suggestion to the minister.
He stated this afternoon that, as originally drafted, section 8 was not in the bill, but, that, having heard discussions from some quarters which he did not indicate, he decided that there should be provision for a report to parliament. I congratulate him upon the change of mind, because a billion dollars, whether it be by [DOT]way of gift, barter, sale, or what-not, is a transaction of great magnitude, and when it comes out of the taxpayers or through borrowings from our citizenship, and when it is expended by a committee of the cabinet, the taxpayers through their representatives are entitled to some kind of report, good, bad or indifferent. The minister has yielded to what he heard and has included in this bill section 8, which provides:	[DOT]
As soon as practicable after the close of each fiscal year, the board shall prepare and lay before parliament a report of operations under this act. . . .
I submit that the section should stop right there. In peace time it would stop there, and in peace time there would be no limitations on it. Now what have we? We have the limitation imposed by the second clause of this section 8, which provides that the report shall be prepared and laid before parliament, but that it shall not contain-*
. . . such information as the governor in council deems it incompatible with the public interest to disclose.
I regret the use of that language. It is a cloak behind which governments, ever since this war began, and perhaps anterior to' this war, have sought to refuse information to parliament. "It is not in the public interest"; that is the only answer you get; and I submit that it is not an answer, it is an arbitrary dictum.
I have a suggestion to make. If it is considered in the interests of public safety, of national safety during war time, of war strategy that certain information shall not be divulged to parliament in the report which it is proposed shall be made under section 8, it should be guarded in that respect and
limited to these two aspects, but it should not be left in the language of this clause to be refused by the arbitrary ipse dixit of the ministry, based upon no other consideration than arbitrariness. I do not assume that information would be refused on a purely arbitrary basis, but it is possible. The matter ought to be based on some reasonable grounds, and I am suggesting two reasonable grounds to the minister. I have not taken the time to draft a substitute clause, but I suggest this as a basis for his consideration overnight, that the clause proceed as it does in lines 39, 40 and 41, down to the word "act," that the limitation now there be expunged, and that there be substituted in lieu thereof an exception or a limitation which would provide "if, in the view of the governor in council, it is inexpedient for reasons of public or national safety or for strategical considerations that such information be brought down in the report tabled to parliament." I suggest to the minister that this is a wholly reasonable view and that he ought to accept the suggestion.

May I interpose. I was only taking the example which had been offered by the last speaker. I am not stating that it did occur. I am. assuming that the illustration he gave was correct. However, if it is not correct we can take it as a hypothetical case. All I say is, I believe that there have been, times when mere lethargy has induced members of the cabinet to refuse information, and instead of giving lethargy as the reason they have stated, "not in the public interest". I do not think most of these refusals have been very important; nevertheless I believe we have seen that from time to time. Therefore, if any change can be made to satisfy the criticism that has been offered, it will be well. I do not agree with that particular criticism, in this way, that I do not think there would be much chance of important information being withheld on that account. In other words, I have pretty complete trust in the government on the. more important matters. But whenever there is something which a minister views as not

very important he will just pull our leg and say it is not in. the public interest for him to give the information. I have great trust in the government on the main issues, but ' on all these details I have not very much trust at all. I think they just kid the house along at- will.
The chief reason why I wish to make a few remarks with respect to the terms of the bill is my desire to deal with the general question of the repatriation of securities and one or two of the reasons given against repatriation of these securities and other paper of that kind. Perhaps I can most easily and quickly express the ideas I have in mind by saying that the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) this afternoon made what I consider to be a most reasonable, unusually lucid and logical speech, with which I entirely agree; or if I do not entirely agree, at any rate, certainly in the main, what he said is in accord with the views I hold. Probably he knew, when he started, that it would not be very long after he had got going before his loyalty to the empire would be impugned; and if it has not been seriously impugned as yet, we may depend upon, it that he will be charged almost with sedition before much time goes by. Naturally, it would be rather difficult for the superimperialists to swallow the sound logic which the hon. member exhibited in that speech. For my part I entirely agree with him when he says that if it is convenient, if it does no one of our partner nations any harm, then there is nothing wrong with obtaining some quid pro quo for what we give.
Of course, I do not think we can give these supplies to Britain or to any other country on the basis of cash-on-the-barrel-head, for the one simple reason introduced by the minister last evening when he said that it would be unthinkable for us to extract pay on every occasion, when the United States had already got away from any such attitude in the matter of giving supplies. Nevertheless there is no reason why a sound business attitude cannot be taken with reference to the contribution which we are to make.
I wish to follow up these remarks by adverting to one of the reasons given for not obtaining certain securities from, say, the old country, and that reason is that it would be well for Canada to remain in debt-not as indebted to a government, but as individuals in debt to individuals-so that there will be a balance of payments with respect to interest going from Canada to the old country. It is said it would be well that we should be in debt in that fashion to the old country, because if

Mutual Aid Bill
we are not thus in debt to the old country she will not perhaps buy from us to the extent that she would buy from a nation which was in debt to her. And plenty of other nations will be in debt. Therefore, when the time comes, it will be thus more difficult for Canada to sell her goods to the old country than would be the case if she were a debtor.
It seems to me there is another reason why a nation like Britain would buy from Canada, and that reason is that Canada would buy from her. These are two of the agencies that contribute toward the creation of trade between nations: one, that they have to take up a balance of payments arising from the debtor position of the country which desires to sell; the other reason being that a nation will buy from a country which has effected a balance of payments by making purchases from it, or which will make purchases from it. I think it is quite clear to a large number of people who are watching the situation from western Canada, which is the great exporting section of the dominion, that there are others who want to have a debt flowing over to the old country in order to have them buy from us, because if they do not have that situation, then the customers of this country will be able to put up the argument, with the greater force, that we had better buy, that wfe had better let some of those other goods in. Those people who want to keep the debt situation in being and keep the securities in Britain realize that, if we do not, the exporters in this country will have a stronger argument in favour of importing from the country that they call the mother country.
So far as this bill is concerned I will support it if we make up our mind never under any circumstances to take back any securities. I would support this or any other measure giving everything we have. But I would not have any industrialist think we are completely blind to what is in his mind when he is talking patriotism and mother love and urging that we should not take securities back into this country. The real reason for that attitude is to keep this country in debt to another country, individual to individual, to keep the balance of-payments with respect to debt, so that the exporter in this country will not be given an additional argument as to the wisdom of importing here. Hon. members can talk about leaving securities in the old country because that is the patriotic thing to do, but the real reason in the mind of almost all the people who want securities left there is that they do not wish to take any chance of an exporter having an argument in favour 'of importing the other country's goods. There may be some hon. members who are fooling
themselves, but I want to tell them now that so far as the large majority of the people in western Canada are concerned they are not being fooled. The reason behind this argument is not patriotism but to keep for themselves the preferred position they have hitherto been able to keep in this country.

I am not rising a second time during the day only for the purpose of thanking the hon. member who has just spoken for having approved what I said this afternoon, but I will avail myself of the opportunity to do so. I am glad that there is at least one hon. member who shares some of the views I have expressed.
While not at all qualifying my approval of the bill but in order to insist that we should avail ourselves of subsection 2 of section 4 of this bill to get some reciprocal benefit, I intend to mention again the question of Labrador for fear that opportunity may not be given to me again, and I ask the indulgence of the committee to carry on for a few minutes on that matter. In fact, had I known the rules of the house better, I would have been able to conclude my remarks this afternoon.
In the first few days of the session when I stated my approval of the bill in principle, I mentioned that we might, well avail ourselves of this occasion to enter into some negotiations with the government of Great Britain for the return of the lands handed over to Newfoundland by the privy council in 1926-27. A few days afterwards the question was brought up in the Quebec house, and a few days later again the hon. member for Gaspe brought it up here. The Prime Minister said then that this question would have to be decided by the people of Newfoundland. I have the greatest respect and the greatest admiration for my leader, but I venture to say that Newfoundland is now a crown colony, not by an act of God but by action of the parliament of Newfoundland.. In 1929 the parliament of Newfoundland, on account of the fact that they could not meet some of their obligations, appealed to the dominions' office for an investigation. A commissioner-I think his name was Amulree-was sent over; he made a report, and upon that report the parliament of Newfoundland presented a petition to the British government to put them in the status of a crown colony. They passed an act of their parliament to that effect. This was afterwards ratified by an act of the British parliament. In regard to that, what I said this afternoon about reciprocity and about consideration in a sentimental way of practical questions should be kept in mind. When the bill was brought before the British parliament asking that the
Mutual Aid Bill

mother country, as she is still called in Toronto, would assume the debts and obligations of Newfoundland, the labour leader, Mr. Clement Attlee, rose in his place in the British house and said, "We will give approval to the bill but what we do not want is to guarantee the money lent to the government of Newfoundland by its lenders, who probably investigated what they were doing before they did it; these lenders concluded a transaction which at the moment may look bad, but they knew what they were doing, and now they want the people of Britain to protect their investment." That was their attitude then. That was not a sentimental objection. Newfoundland had always been a. devoted and loyal crown colony and it had become afterwards a loyal dominion; yet a gentleman, who is now a member of the present government in Britain and who was then the labour party leader, interposed to say that the British people should not be made responsible for investments made by some people in Newfoundland bonds.
I would also mention the fact that certain military bases were given by Britain to the United States in return for a certain number of destroyers; a fair business exchange. Let us say they were leased for ninety-nine years, but there is great danger that this might last longer. Anyway this is the span of a few generations. Were the people of Newfoundland consulted by plebiscite or otherwise before giving those bases? I do not think they were.
A reason advanced in favour of the measure we are now debating is that it would contribute to the victory of the allied nations. We have already done so handsomely. We voted $2,135,000,000 last year besides the grant of a billion dollars and we will vote more this year. I am in favour of what has been done, but that should not stop us from remembering that there are other considerations to be taken into account. Why should not some contribution be expected from Newfoundland, and why should not the government of Britain, which now through the dominions' office controls this crown colony, be expected to enter into negotiations with us? Labrador was not regarded as being worth a billion dollars a few years ago. It is known that in- 1924, before the case reached the privy council, there was a meeting in Montreal at which were present representatives of the federal government, and of the provincial government of Quebec. Mr. Taschereau and his deputy minister were present, and one legal representative was Mr. Plaxton of the federal Department of Justice.
[Mr. Picard.)
These people represented the Canadian interest. Prime Minister Munroe of Newfoundland and his colonial secretary were present, as was also Mr. Magratb who was later in charge of this Labrador case for Newfoundland before the privy council. At that time it was disclosed, and later more officially, that Mr. Munroe mentioned as a possible price for the acquisition by Canada of any rights Newfoundland may have had to Labrador, an amount of $30,000,000, which- later was possibly reduced to $15,000,000.
I have personal recollection in my early days, when I was a humble. secretary to the then Minister of Justice, of a man entering my office and to my great amazement saying to me, "What about buying Labrador?" Of course that was great news to me. He produced letters authorizing him to negotiate with- the Canadian government authorities for an agreement for the purchase of Labrador by Canada. At that moment they were down to $15,000,000, or at least that is what I was told. That man- was not then heard by the minister or, I think, by the government, but he put his proposals in writing, whether in a private letter or otherwise. I remember -him very well, because his name was the same as that of the founder of Quebec; it was de Champlain. He came to the government privately warning us, "You know, we will get a favourable judgment from the privy council in a couple of years, and the price will go up." In the senate in 1935 the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen admitted that in 1931, a few years after the judgment of the privy council had been rendered, the government of Newfoundland wanted $100,000,000 for Labrador. Therefore that judgment raised the price; when they were sure Labrador was theirs, the price went up. Even if the price remains at $100,000,000, that is far less than $1,000,000,000; and if we are willing to give a billion, I should think the people of Newfoundland might be willing to sacrifice ten per cent of what we are giving.
This question of Labrador might be looked at also from the historical point of view. Newfoundland had been British for fifty years before Labrador became British. At that time Newfoundland had no control, over Labrador, which was part of the French territories which were ceded to Britain by the treaty of Paris in February, 1763. It was only eight or nine months later, in October, 1763, that the British government by proclamation placed Labrador under the jurisdiction of Newfoundland instead of under

Mutual Aid Bill
the British governor of Quebec. In 1774 Labrador was again transferred from the governor of Newfoundland to the governor of Quebec, or the local legislative council or sovereign council that then existed Then, after being governed by the sovereign council in Quebec under the British governor for thirty-five years, Labrador was again transferred by the British government to the jurisdiction of the authorities of Newfoundland. That was in 1809. So that there has been a constant transfer of that territory which we might well repeat at this moment. There is nothing disloyal in making this suggestion. Sixteen years later, in 1825, this arrangement was not found adequate for part of Labrador, and that part on the shores of the gulf as far down as a place called Blanc Sablon was again transferred to the jurisdiction of the government of Quebec. Of course it will be said that this was before Newfoundland had dominion status, but it goes to show that these territories have been handed back and forth between the Canadian and Newfoundland authorities, so that there is no reason for surprise that we should now ask for a reconsideration of the arrangement. I do not think any Canadian should oppose it, because the values there are immense. Remember that Alaska was bought by the United States from Russia in 1867 for $7,500,000, and it was not long before Alaska was bringing in that much and more in income each year from the fisheries, the mines and so on; and Alaska is now one of our greatest bases for offence and defence on the western end of our hemisphere.
Therefore, I do not think it would be a bad thing for this country to negotiate in an attempt to secure the resources and wealth to be found in Labrador, which has immense forests, water power, mines and what-not I do not think anyone should blame me for bringing forward this question. It is not the matter of a sale. I do not want to place any new items in this bill, as was suggested a moment ago by one hon. member, so that this will look like bargain hunting. I am perfectly satisfied with what is in the bill now, but I am suggesting that the government might avail itself of one of the sections already in this bill, which I read this afternoon, section 2 of paragraph 4, and enter into negotiations with the British government who might be called to act in the same spirit of charitable enterprise, in an attempt to get back these territories and these resources which, after all, will offer some compensation for what we are doing in this bill. I do not recall nor do I qualify my approval of this
measure. I am simply suggesting that we should act in a practical way, as other nations do, and proceed on a sound basis, at the same time contributing to the victory of our allies and to our own safety.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
There are three or four features of this bill to which I should like to refer for a few minutes, dealing with sections 4 to 8 particularly. We are in our infancy in this lease-lend legislation; I believe we are the first dominion to have such a bill. As I mentioned this afternoon, in the United States they have an administrator of their lease-lend programme. We had the same principle in the last war; we had private administration in the munitions board, with a chairman, which handled all the work now being carried on by the Minister of Munitions and Supply.
This bill provides that "united nations" shall mean the signatories to the declaration made at Washington on January 1, 1942. Let us not forget that twenty-six nations signed the Brussels agreement and the Nyon pact about the Mediterranean sea and piracy, and Great Britain was the only one to carry them out. Let us remember that several nations signed an agreement with respect to Poland, and then left Britain to hold the bag. Do not forget that certain other nations may be brought within the terms of this legislation by order in council. We must remember that Russia is not at war with Japan, that China is not at war with Germany, and that since January 1, 1942, several South American countries have come into the war. What about them?
Last November, December and February some questions arose in Britain as to the distribution of certain funds and over priorities in the various theatres of war. We all know that the distribution and administration of funds often bring about great difficulties. It was said in the British house that the Lady Cripps fund for China was not being administered in the proper way and should be left for distribution to the International Red Cross. In a recent report as to distribution to the government at Washington, the American Red Cross in 1938 recommended that the distribution of certain supplies in China should be handled by the International Red Cross.
I may say that I agree with the hon. member for York-Sunbury in regard to the set-up of the board, and that the board should have power to make supplies available to the united nations; it is thus giving orders in council the force of statutes, and I agree that section 4 (2) should end with the word "war" in line 45. In regard to the set-up of the board, I think it is a great mistake in the
Mutual Aid Bill

fourth year of the war to adopt a principle, in regard to lease-lend which will no doubt apply after the war, to be applied to rebuilding the devastated countries. Do not forget that when the war is over, we may have, with the other allied nations, to supply all these nations in Europe with foodstuffs, munitions and everything of that kind. Under this Bill No. 76 the same principle will apply after the war. The same principle will apply to the rebuilding of those nations which have been destroyed by the axis powers.
This question was raised in the British House of Commons last fall and early in January. After the fall of Singapore the question was brought up in that house. The government was asked who was to decide on the priorities to be granted to the various theatres of war regarding the army, navy, air force and munitions. There had been considerable criticism in New Zealand and Australia and throughout the far east as to these decisions being given against them without their knowledge of what was going on. The Prime Minister of Great Britain said that there was not sufficient to go around and that it was his duty as head of the government to decide the countries that should receive supplies and priorities. We are going to fall into the same pitfall in connection with this particular bill.
It is set out in section 3(1) that a committee of the cabinet will be set up as a Canadian Mutual Aid board, but I think that is wrong. I would point out to the Minister of Finance that to-day there are four neutral countries in Europe. One is the Irish Free State. The other is Turkey which is thinking of coming into the war. Then there are Spain and Sweden. These four neutrals have stayed or sat on the fence so far. Turkey was against us in the last war. How are supplies that may go to these countries to be treated if our board says so later? Under this bill the governor- in council can lay down rules and regulations which would permit these countries or any others later to receive supplies. Spain has received supplies since the war started because it was thought that this was necessary in order to keep her in line. There are also the other republics to be considered.
I think the annual report should be made to parliament within fifteen days. The principal raised by loan under this bill and the interest thereon are to be a "charge upon the consolidated revenue fund. There are other objections to this particular set-up. The reason why we won in Africa is that proper preparations were made. When we started that cam1 paign under General Waved, that great soldier, there were not sufficient munitions or tanks or
supplies. These had to be brought around the cape of Good Hope, up through the Indian ocean, through the Red sea and the Suez canal. After they got the proper equipment they were able to march 1,600 miles to win the campaign.
Objection has been made in England to having a set-up like this. As Sir Robert Borden once said, the governor in council in any event is a political board under the constitution and it will always remain one. I think it would be better if -the government made some changes in the bill. In my opinion there should be an independent body to decide how the fund will be distributed. After all, that is the gist of the whole bill. Military strategy, not political strategy, should be the first consideration. This is what New Zealand and Australia are complaining about in the far east when they wanted to revive the empire war cabinet of the last war in this war.
I fail to see why the neutral nations which sat on the fence should be able to come in under this bill the same as other countries. I think -the bill in its present form will prove dangerous in the future when we are assisting in the rebuilding of Europe and as to what later on the South American countries will get. No doubt that work will have to be carried out under lend-lease, mainly by Great Britain, Russia and the United States, but the dominions will be brought in. I fear that this will be taken as a precedent in the future.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister a number of questions. These are general in character and are chiefly applicable to section 1, and I think I should be allowed to ask them now. First, would the minister explain at somewhat greater length than he did this afternoon why there has been a change in the mechanism of our contribution under Mutual Aid. Under the billion dollar gift we allocated a certain sum of money to Great Britain which she used freely to purchase what she chose in Canada in the way of goods, supplies and foodstuffs. We have discarded that method and are now allocating to Great Britain, and to other united nations, such goods as are deemed to be strategically necessitous. We in Canada, through this board which is to be set up, will handle the actual allocation instead of granting a certain sum of money and leaving the choice of the materials to the countries which are to use them. I think the reasons for this change should be stated fully to the committee.
I should like to know whether the fact that Great Britain was criticized for sending some

Mutual Aid Bill
of the materials which she received from Canada to others of our fighting allies, perhaps with some financial offset in the complicated international transactions which are taking place, was one of the reasons for this change in the mechanism to be used under this Mutual Aid bill.
My second question is rather a minor one.
I should like to know who bore the marine risk in connection with goods which were sent to Great Britain and to the other financial fronts under the billion dollar gift. Were all goods sent at Great Britain's risk and none at Canada's? I should like to know also how we service our own troops in Great Britain and other points in the world wherever they may be. Do we bear the marine risk of sending foodstuffs and munitions to our troops? Is this done by means of sending goods to England and then having England look after our troops? In other words, has Canada had any risks or any losses on account of enemy action on the ocean? I am speaking, of course, of ships not owned by ourselves. Do we carry marine insurance and pay premiums? If so, do we come under the British government scheme of marine insurance?
The next question is: What if the tide of international payments goes against Canada in favour of England?

speechtext:
Do I hear someone ask "how"? I shall read a short paragraph from a publication as follows:
The conditions which were met by the U.K. financing act are not expected to recur. A European offensive in 1943, bringing the Canadian first army into action from its British bases, would mean a sharp rise in Canadian army expenditures in Great Britain. This is counted on to reverse the trend that has created a huge British deficit of Canadian dollars.
In other words, I think this committee is entitled to know what is the reasonable expectation in regard to Canadian dollars versus sterling if our troops should see action this year.
The next question is, will this committee get a break-down of the balance of exchange payments with the United States similar to the table which the minister presented to the committee this afternoon in regard to our exchange with Great Britain? Some years ago we had this question of United States exchange versus the Canadian dollar before the house during a budget debate or a debate on one of
the special acts that we passed, and at that time the matter was treated with great secrecy, perhaps needlessly so in the light of subsequent events. But now that we have been given a break-down of sterling exchange as against the Canadian dollar, surely we are entitled to a break-down of United States exchange as against the Canadian dollar.
I should like to know just what effect this new method of allocation will have in regard to our United States exchange. Under the Hyde Park agreement I believe Canada was very favourably treated. I shall not go into details, because they may be mostly surmises on my part as to exactly how they operated, but I have always understood1 that Canada was given specially favourable treatment in order that she might have enough United States exchange to meet our payments to the United States.
A question which arose out of the billion dollar gift to Great Britain last year and the taking of securities back, in particular the loan of $700,000,000 against the collateral of British-held Canadian securities, is this. When that loan was made I understood, perhaps wrongly, that the amount of the loan, namely $700,000,000 was about equal to the then total value of the remaining securities in England. We have heard in the minister's speech introducing the resolution that the value of that loan is about two-thirds of their present value. Does that two-thirds relate to the value as of the time the loan was made, or does it reflect the fact that with the prospect of victory being closer, the values of many securities have risen in Canada and that, therefore, the $700,000,000 is two-thirds of the present value rather than of the then value of the loan? These are questions which I should like to have answered so that we might proceed with the various sections more intelligently.

The questions asked by the hon. member for Rosedale are the .following. First explain why the change in the mechanism has been made; why not follow the practice of last year's bill and make another billion dollar gift? I tried to answer that question in advance in the speech in which I. introduced the resolution. After I pointed out that we have now diplomatic relations with many of these countries, including Russia and China, as well as the British dominions, I said:
This will make direct assistance to them easy. Moreover, our potential transactions with several of these countries are quite substantial and we feel it is desirable in matters of such importance that we ourselves give full consideration to the terms on which such transfers should be made.
That is reason No. 1. We wanted to determine the terms instead of leaving it to someone else.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: May I ask why the minister feels that we can more usefully determine the destination here than it can be done by the allocation boards sitting in Washington or London? Not that I am not a supporter of Canada becoming a full-fledged nation in every way. Nevertheless there are export boards dealing with supplies on a vaster scale than our own contribution, and looking at the board to be set up under this act, while it is an eminently capable board in many ways, it is perhaps more capable in other fields than in the allocation of supplies for military purposes. Is this to satisfy our sense of sovereignty, or is there some real reason for setting up our own allocation board rather than having this done by the allocation boards sitting in Washington and London?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: I do not think it will be done less well by us, and if there is no inequality in efficiency we should certainly do it ourselves. This Mutual Aid board will have to be closely in touch with the munitions assignment boards. We must control the destination and terms, we think, but w'e must not cross wires with these munitions assignment boards, and that means that it would be absolutely necessary to be closely in touch with those boards, especially the one sitting in Washington.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES

speechtext: Just what does the minister mean by saying that we must control the terms?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: There will be terms. Section 4 of the bill enables the Mutual Aid board and/or the governor in council to fix the terms and conditions on which the war supplies are furnished. I have given as an instance two or three times that ships might be returned. It is hard to visualize all the terms and conditions that one might wish to stipulate. In some instances it might be some privileges in the country concerned, the use of some ports or air fields on certain terms, or something of that kind. I am just speculating. One does not know what might arise. But at any rate the determination of the terms should be a matter for the dominion government rather than for another government.

speechtext: Hear, hear. I agree entirely.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: We feel sorry for the ministers in the amount of work that they heap upon themselves when they create one board after another and constitute themselves members of it. All these things require not only a tremendous amount of work but a specialized background. Coupled with my feeling of sympathy for ministers who become members of these boards, and particularly the leading ministers, is a feeling of despair as to how the affairs of the country can be well managed when so few try to do so much. It seems to me it might be better to have a greater division of the work; and if there is a system functioning reasonably satisfactorily already under present allocationary boards, I am not one who would be eager to heap more work on the shoulders of already overworked ministers.	[DOT]

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES

-and for a quiet life you try to remove grounds for criticism, whether it is just or unjust. The second reason is that we think it is important that the Canadian source of this assistance should be clear to the countries receiving it and that Canada should deal with them direct. that they should not be channeled or routed through another country. Those are, I think, the main reasons for making the change in the mechanism.

This

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: That would work in this way: Britain, perhaps, would also help our troops by supplying them with munitions and goods as they are needed.

speechtext: Yes, I know.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
But the balance is against
us: we supply more to them than they supply us, if you consider it separately in that way. But that is not at all the theory of this legislation. They are doing what they can, as much as they can, and we are doing what we can, as much as we can; that is the theory of the legislation.
The next question is, who bears the marine risk of the shipments? The answer to that is that Great Britain does. And, how do we service our troops? We send the goods to Great Britain; Great Britain supplies the troops, and furnishes other requirements we have in England, and the accounts are adjusted in the way I have tried to explain in the various speeches I have made. That means that if in the coming year the amounts

Mutual Aid Bill
obtained in Great Britain are very much greater than they were in the past, the amount transferred in dollars to the British government will be very much greater than it was in the past. It therefore means that their deficit will be very much less than it was in the past, and consequently the amount supplied them under the Mutual Aid measure and chargeable to the Mutual Aid appropriation will be less than it was in the past. If there are operations on a very great scale or on an expensive scale in Great Britain, it might mean such a large payment of Canadian dollars to Great Britain that this billion dollars would be cut down below a billion dollars; that the Mutual Aid would be very much less than that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Before the minister goes on to the next question, would he be more explicit with regard1 to this marine insurance? subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
I do not know when we had the figures here of the balance of payments in connection with the act the minister put through to conserve United States exchange-two years ago probably. We were then given only piecemeal information, and one could make a whole picture out of it only by getting information from commercial and financial sources. But I notice that the Economist of February 20 gives the balance of payments between Canada and the United States, showing that over the four-year period there was a deficit of 8720 millions against Canada. In 1941, the last year given, we had $1,042,000,000 of credits and $1,372,000,000 of debits, and for the three-year period $720,000,000 against us.
If it is not information to the enemy to give the balance of payments as between Canada and Great Britain, surely it is not information to the enemy to give the balance as between the United States and Canada. I would ask the minister, therefore, to be good enough to table these figures at his early convenience.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: The 1941 figures given in the Economist were published in Canada, and the 1942 figures will be some time, but not very soon. I do not wish to make this public now.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Is the minister prepared to say how the exchange is running between Canada and the United States? After all, some of these goods which are the subject matter of this bill will go to the United States or will be at the disposal of the United States for use where the United States troops are. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: I have said at least once in the budget speech and once since that the exchange position is very much easier. The way I put it was that it is no longer one of our major worries.

speechtext:
I have read in the British Hansard that Sir Kingsley Wood has stated in the British house that customs duties were paid on shipments in virtue of the lend-lease bill in the United States and in virtue of the Mutual Aid legislation also. On all that they were receiving they were charging duty. My first question will be: Is that the case? If so, was the duty paid by the Canadian government to the British government on shipments made in virtue of the gift legislation of last year, and is it proposed to do the same this year in virtue of this legislation? My second question is this: Did the government include the amount of our shipments in virtue of the
Mutual Aid Bill

gift legislation of last year, and what was voted in March and so on, in the lists of our exports that have been given to the Canadian public?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES

speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. ILSLEY': The answer is no. Whether the British government paid itself duty on the goods I do not know. We do quite a lot of that ourselves. Mr. ILSLEY':	Our export figures would
include all that we exported, whether paid for out of the billion dollar gift or not. It would include those.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Does the minister not think a distinction should be established1 between exports of Canadian manufactured goods that are sold to other countries and those that are given? When they are given away for war purposes there should be some distinction to show that such trade is not the same as ordinary trade when something is given in return.
Mr. ILSLEY': It should be given consideration. Up to date there would be no reason for doing that under the billion dollar gift because Great Britain bought the goods. True, they used the amount which was placed to their credit by the Canadian government to pay for a large part of it; nevertheless they bought the goods and those were exports sold by an exporter to an importer in every sense of the word. When we begin operating under this act we shall be really delivering goods for considerations other than monetary considerations, and there will not be a price chargeable , by the exporter in this country to the importer in the other country in the same sense, so that the question will arise as to how the return should be made. One way would be to let them go into our figures of exports as usual
[Mr. Pouliot.j
and indicate the price that we pay the producers here, but it may be that this would not be a good way. It is a matter that should receive consideration.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: I have another question. As a rule, with regard to external trade, shipments are made by A in Canada to B in a country abroad, and A and B may mean respectively an individual or a firm or anybody who is in business. With regard to the gift legislation, by whom were the shipments made and what were the distributing agencies in England? Who was receiving the gift in Great Britain and how was the distribution made of food and ammunition? It is easier in the case of ammunition, because ammunition could have been sent direct to the British government; but to whom were the edible exports sent to Great Britain and how were they distributed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: The money was placed to the credit of the United Kingdom government in the Bank of Canada, and shipments were made to the appropriate agencies or departments of the United Kingdom government. Some shipments would go to the food ministry, some to the admiralty, some to the war office, some to the ministry of supply and so on. But it had to go to the United Kingdom government, because it was the United Kingdom government that was buying it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: It was sent direct to the British government?

speechtext:
Y'es.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES

speechtext:
Does the minister not know? Are we collecting from the British government the amount of the freight from the factories to the coast? It would make a material difference to the cost of the goods.
Mr. ILSLEY': I am informed that we have been collecting the freight between the factory and the coast from the British government.
I want to answer one question of the hon. member for Rosedale which I did not answer with regard to securities in Great Britain. In the speech I made last Thursday I said that the $700 million obligation is about two-thirds of the value of the securities outstanding in Great Britain. The latest and best estimate that I can get of the value of the Canadian

Mutual Aid Bill
securities held in Great Britain is $1,066,000,000. Various estimates have been made from time to time of the value of the securities held there. On the basis of the valuation given by the hon. member for Bellechasse this afternoon it would be hard to understand why that figure is not larger than this. But those figures were based upon the last estimate of the dominion bureau of statistics made in 1937 or 1938; it was either made in 1938 based on 1937, or made in 1937, and none has been made since. There may have been a considerable volume of selling. of those securities before the war. There may have been also a considerable change in the value of the securities since that time. I think those 1937 values were high; I think in a great many cases they took the values at par or when stocks were far below par; they took book values and one thing and another, and got too high a value.
Mr. LaCROIX (Quebec-Montmorency): Has the minister any idea what percentage of the capital of the Canadian Pacific is held over there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
No; I do not know. Of course there has been a very substantial repatriation. Those railway securities, a list of which the hon. member for Bellechasse read this afternoon, included Canadian National railway securities. Including private repatriation, we have repatriated $800 million worth of those securities. When all these things are considered the figure of $1,066,000,000 that I have given, which is, as I say, the very latest and best valuation I can get of the securities, is explained. Of that amount, $586,900,000 are Canadian dollar securities and $479,200,000 are sterling securities.
The hon. member for Rosedale said he understood me to say last year that the $700 million covered the value of the securities in England. Apparently I made a very conservative statement; I said the 8700 million covered the dollar securities. I now find that the value of the dollar securities is $5S6,900,000.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Ever since the war broke out, Russia has been an increasingly great purchaser of machine tools, and will continue to be. Under this new lend-lease bill will Canada be in a position to ship machine tools direct to Russia? If so, what effort will be made to provide Canadian manufacturers of machine tools with opportunity to supply Russia? To-day we .are one of the great machine tool manufacturers of the world; perhaps the United States and Great Britain alone surpass us in capacity. If Canada can now deal directly with Russia under this bill, what I should like the minister to tell the committee is, what effort will be made to see that
our machine tool manufacturers supply direct to Russia the machine tools that she very greatly needs and will continue to need?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Under this bill what would happen is, the representative of the . Soviet union would come to the Mutual Aid board and state their requirements of machine tools. If the manufacture and supply of those machine tools could be arranged, and it was deemed to be the most appropriate use of our production and transportation facilities, having in mind the war needs, the Department of Munitions and Supply would arrange for the manufacture of those machine tools, and between the board and the Soviet union they w'ould see that the tools werq transported there on such terms as might be agreed between the board and the government of the Soviet union.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Could we not go a step further? Instead of waiting for the representative of the Soviet union to apply to whatever board is set up to administer this legislation, why could we not approach the Soviet union? No doubt they know the capacity of our machine tool factories to-day. One of the largest in the world is the Bertram plant at Dundas, Ontario, and there are other great manufacturers of munitions which, of course, after the war will go into machine tools.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: I do not think it is a case of going looking for orders. I think the governments of the united nations are all very much alive to their needs and very much aware of the possibilities of having those needs met. I would anticipate that if there were any need for machine tools by Russia, and Canada could make them, Russia would know' it and would approach us.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: And they could purchase them under our lend-lease legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: As I said before, that would depend upon a number of factors. I do not know' whether they could or not. If the board decided that that was the most appropriate and suitable use to make of our production and transportation facilities, having in mind the wrar needs as a whole, then I have no doubt they would get the tools on such terms as might be agreed on.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES

Mutual Aid Bill

speechtext:
The minister will tell me
if I am trespassing on the time of the committee, and if he says so I will pay heed to him, but this afternoon he was good enough to furnish the committee with a statement which contains two tables that are not clear to me. On the first page, in the upper part, we have the break-down which brings it out at exactly 81,000,000,000. Then under the heading, "Remaining portion attributed arbitrarily to other sources of financing" we have an additional $440,000,000. May I ask whether that $440,000,000 so styled was a gift in addition to the billion dollars, or whether that amount of money was paid by Britain, and if that is what the title means?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Oh, no. This covers substantially a period of nine months, from April 1 to the time the gift ran out, which was in the latter part of December. During that time we supplied $1,440,000,000 worth of goods, services and so on, or we were paid $1,440,000,000 for the particular purposes set out on this page. Nobody can say what was covered by the billion dollars and what was not covered, because the $1,440,000,000 came from two sources. It came from the billion dollar gift, and it came from the other normal sources which Great Britain has for Canadian dollars, namely exports to Canada, the supplying of services and so on. Therefore, with many apologies this afternoon, I explained
[Mr. Douglas G. Ross.l
that while I was putting this on record, I had no right arbitrarily to place those items under the billion dollar gift. I could have taken almost any other items and put them under it. I did not know whether this would make it clear or more confusing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES

Perhaps I may add a word or two to shorten the discussion. Britain can buy anything she likes in this country. What we gave a year ago was a credit of a billion dollars. Britain, of course, creates certain credits of her own in various ways, by exports and by counter-expenditures for Canada in the United Kingdom; and beyond that her credit is good. If she wants to go in debt to us beyond that, she can do so. The result is that we sell Britain what Britain asks for from this country, and I think it is very difficult to give a list.
The discussion leads me to believe that many hon. members think we do a sort of retail business in munitions; that we take a gun off a shelf and give it to Britain and say, "Here is a gun." As a matter of fact, what
actually happens is -that we permit Britain to place an order in Canada with some Canadian factory. I am the authorized agent for Britain, as Minister of Munitions and Supply, to handle those matters. If Britain wants 500 guns here, she authorizes me to place a'contract with a Canadian factory for 500 guns. A Canadian inspector then takes charge of the order and follows it from the raw metal -through to the finished product. Then Britain may instruct us to put them in storage in Canada or send them to Halifax for transhipment overseas. They are her guns, from the time they start as molten metal until they are delivered. She is simply a buyer in our factories, so far as the mechanics of the -thing go. I do not think you could trace the billion dollar credit into the actual munitions covered by that credit; I do not think you can distinguish that credit from other credits Britain has in this country. I think that is the difficulty of saying that it does include this and does not include that.

speechtext:
Now that the Minister
of Munitions and Supply is willing to answer questions-I do not mean for one moment that he has been unwilling-I should like to ask him a few. I thought we were to refer our questions to the Minister of Finance. I am not satisfied with the completeness of the answer given by the Minister of Finance with regard to the machine tool industry being able to supply the wants of any of our allies under the new lend-lease arrangement. The Minister of Munitions and Supply is familiar with the machine tool business. I am also thoroughly familiar with that industry, and I know many manufacturers are

looking with anxiety to the future and wondering whether they will be invited to supply, say Russia and other allies. I should be glad to hear from the Minister of Munitions and Supply, for I know he knows, just how the manufacturers of machine tools in Canada will be able to operate under this new lend-lease bill. There are many factories in Toronto, Hamilton, Galt and elsewhere in Canada which manufacture fine machine tools and which are able to go outside Canada for business along some lines, if not along all at the present time. Will Canada now be able to solicit business from those of our allies who may want machine tools?

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Applications from allied governments will come to the board being set up under this bill. It will be the duty of that board to discuss with other producing countries, mainly the United States and Britain, whether the request should be met and also decide which country should meet the request. We might get a request for machine tools which would overlap a request made to the United States, and in that event the duplication would be cleared. A request may come to Canada, and it may be found that for shipping reasons or idle capacity it would be preferable to fill the requisition in Britain or the United States. If it should be decided that the transaction is properly an item that Canada should fill, and Canada agrees that she is able to fill it, then the Department of Munitions and Supply would arrange for its manufacture and shipment to the government to which it is assigned. The solicitation of foreign governments is a thing of the past. Whether we keep the machine tool industry operating at capacity will depend upon whether that' is the most urgent production. We have only so many men, and we have only so much raw material. We may decide that it would be better to devote the productive capacity of the machine tool industry to the building of ships or the manufacture of aircraft. That is a matter which would have to be determined, in the first instance by the board and in the second instance by the Department of Munitions and Supply. The day of competitive business for profit does not exist at all at the moment. The main effort will be to get the greatest and most useful capacity out of Canadian industries.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
I am not concerned about what commodities go into this account. If Great Britain wants something, let her have it. It is the value of the commodities that we must be more concerned about in connection with this gift.
I should like to ask the minister a question which has been upon my mind for some time and which was brought up again by a letter I received from one of my farmer constituents and having to do with this particular matter. It is not so much the total amount of the evaluation of these commodities that I am concerned about as a representative of the people. The minister and his department are, I know, concerned about the administrative end of the bill, but the people of Canada look at this matter in a different manner. They say: We are giving so much to the united nations; how much are we getting for it? How much is the total amount valued at on the books of the department? For instance, we find that ninety million bushels of wheat were sent to some country or another in the sterling area and that about $77,500,000 was received for it. The question that concerns the farmer is, how much do I get for that? These goods are given to Britain.
The point I am coming to is this. This year's bill not only involves gifts to Britain but grants power to extend this plan of making gifts to any of the united nations. The United States is doing something very similar to this, the same in principle, shall I say, through its lease-lend operations. The question in the farmer's mind is this: We are all fighting the same war; all the united nations are attempting to defeat the same enemy. Why is it, therefore, that the farmer of the United States should get, say, $1.75 for his wheat that goes through the same channel as my wheat, and yet I and the other farmers in Canada are getting only, say, sixty-five or seventy cents a bushel for our wheat going to the same destination? That is a question which I think should be answered. I have never been able
to justify the position. I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce has often told this house that he cannot reveal the price that we are getting for such a thing or the price involved in some trade agreement. But the position is simply this. The Canadian people are heavily taxed; they are asked to subscribe to war loans; they find themselves part of the general war scheme; and yet here is a certain industry in Canada which is very largely, I think I am right in saying, responsible for supplying most of the commodities that are figured in this account, because the foods, those agricultural and vegetable products and animal and fish products, come for the most part from the basic industry of agriculture. And the farmer of Canada is asking: Why cannot I get more for my products? It is hard for me to get through. My farming neighbour to the south of me across the line is getting twice as much as I am. That is a deserving question, and I hope the minister will throw some light upon it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext:
A point of order was raised by the Minister of Finance. I cannot see how the minister can answer the question put by the hon. member for Macleod. Standing order 58 (2) reads:
