subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Perhaps now that the Minister of Munitions and Supply is here, he will answer the question I addressed to the Minister of Finance as to whether Britain or Canada pays the marine risk insurance on Canadian shipments going to Great Britain. I assume from what the minister of munitions has said to us that any purchase in Canada by Britain is at Britain's own risk, and that that applies not only from the time the ore is being smelted but also to its shipment across the ocean and to the whole proceedings under the billion dollar gift as well as to every dollar's worth of supplies bought under any credits which Britain may have established in Canada. If I am correct in that assumption, I should like the minister to confirm it, and to ask him more particularly who bears the marine risk in connection with the supplies of war materials and foodstuffs which we send to Britain and perhaps to other parts of the

Mutual Aid Bill

world to maintain our own boys in our own army or navy or air force. Does Canada bear that risk of submarine warfare, or does Britain bear it by reason of the fact that she gets foodstuffs through the billion dollar gift, and then allocates some of them for the use of Canadian troops in Great Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: It depends upon who owns the material at the time the ocean is crossed. If it is British material bought in this country with the credit that has been established for Britain in Canada, the material is shipped not only over our own railroads but over the ocean at the expense of Britain. It is her material and she makes her own shipping arrangements. She not only pays the cost of transportation across the Atlantic but pays the insurance, if she insures. Similarly, if it is Canadian material being sent over for Canadian account to our own troops, all shipping arrangements are made by Canada. Canada charters the shipping space, pays the cost of insuring the goods, if she insures them, and pays the cost of transportation. It all depends upon who owns the material at the time it is shipped.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Now' that the principles are established, I wonder if the minister would illustrate the actual facts of the case. I am in entire agreement with the principles. Have we in Canada suffered the loss of any shipments by reason of submarine warfare? I do not want to know the amount. Have the losses been extensive for Canada, or has practically all the ocean-borne traffic that has been lost been for the account of Great Britain? I think the minister will understand what I am driving at.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Of course we have our own Canadian ships plying across the Atlantic and usually carrying Canadian-owned material. That fleet, I am happy to say, is still intact, but we have shipped material on other ships that have been sunk, and we have, of course, collected insurance on the cargo.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Who feeds our Canadian army?

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: It is fed by arrangement with the British government, and we pay the British government for the supplies. That is the only practical way.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
We do not know just how terrific the losses of shipping have been through submarine warfare. It is a very great problem, and it is of considerable interest to the people of this country to know whether or not we bear any share of that loss, or if it is all borne by Great Britain. If Great Britain feeds and clothes and otherwise looks after our Canadian

troops, of whom there is a very goodly number in Britain, and we only pay for those goods and foodstuffs that are safely delivered, there must be a tremendous loss to Great Britain by reason of submarine warfare and also by reason of the fact that we are only paying a fair price for the delivered article which does not take into account the risk of loss which is occasioned in getting the goods over there. A great many of the goods go to the bottom of the ocean. Is what I have stated a fact, that Great Britain has, virtually at any rate- we will not quibble about the exceptional case here and there-borne the whole risk of the ocean transportation in regard to the feeding, clothing and equipping of our troops overseas?

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Surely the insurance would be an item of cost that would be reckoned in the price of the goods on the other side.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Well, under present conditions it is hard to know.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: The price of wheat in Britain would be the price of wheat in Canada, plus freight and insurance to Britain, plus loading and unloading charges. It always has been, and I think it still is. If the losses are heavy, assuming that the insurance rates are adequate, they would be high and the price would be more; if losses are light, the insurance and prices would be adjusted accordingly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: That would be so if it were a straight business transaction. But presumably it is different now.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: No different now from what it ever was. The rates vary with the risk.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
But governments now
run all this business. Apparently the Minister of Munitions and Supply runs most of the business of Canada-more than half of it- and perhaps deserves credit here and there for doing so. Nevertheless, to take one example, our air force in Great Britain must consume a tremendous amount of gasoline. The price of gasoline in peace time, when there is an abundant supply and competition obtains, is readily determined. At the present time I should think the price of a gallon of gasoline in England is almost any price which the government cares to set on it. As I see it, there are no fixed commercial competitive prices for these articles which must be supplied to our armed services overseas. Prices must be fairly arbitrary, fixed by the British government. We did not have the submarine risk prior to the war, and since then we have had the great cost of this additional risk that must be put into the cost of the article, but at what rate one does not know. There is no

Mutual Aid Bill
competition to regulate it. It must be an arbitrary price. It seems to me that if Britain wanted she could charge, for a gallon of gasoline servicing one of our aircraft over there, whatever price she liked in sterling, so that the result might easily be that England would not be owing us money, but that we would be owing Great Britain money. I think the minister will understand that there must be something in my contention. We are not familiar with the actual operation, just how things go, but ordinary business principles do not obtain.
I am particularly interested in knowing whether we are bearing directly or indirectly any of the risk of ocean transportation, because it is a major factor in the cost of the supplies to-day. In fact, the minister might even bear me out if I were to make a supposititious statement and say that the risks of ocean insurance double the ordinary cost of goods in Great Britain, which goods must be used in large part for the servicing of our own troops. I am endeavouring to measure, as closely as one can approximate things, what the contribution of Great Britain is to this war in regard to servicing Canada. We have given Great Britain a sum of money, a credit, for which we are entitled to credit, and now we are allocating goods to Great Britain. I want to find out, in regard to our own troops, just what contribution Britain is making and what losses she is suffering through ocean transportation.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
We maintain a large staff
of chartered accountants in England to determine exactly what the costs are. Certainly it is the intention of the Canadian government and of the British government that the costs will be the actual costs and that no losses shall be involved to anyone. For instance, if gasoline is charged at a certain price, I think our accountants will ask the British government to establish the basis of the cost, and that will certainly include insurance. I can assure my hon. friend that it will not be forgotten. I know something about war risk insurance myself, and I know it is a very, very considerable item in every transaction. Just as every shipment in this country is checked for cost from the source to the delivery point, I am sure that every consignment from this country to Britain is checked for cost.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
The minister, who at one time held the portfolio of Minister of Transport, knows that even in our own railways there is no basis for fixing freight rates except what the traffic will bear. We cannot be scientific about prices at all times. What you can get for a thing is the ordinary deter-
72537-1641	[DOT]
minant of price. Here we are at war; and what Britain can get for goods in the old country where they are required, or in Africa, is just about whatever price she wants to fix, except that we trust to her fairness. But I do not think any set of accountants, cost accountants or others, can possibly fix prices by actual costs. Who knows what it takes to keep up the Royal Navy, the air force and all these other indirect items which the minister knows so well must be allocated over the units. He will understand the accounting language, anyway. The whole thing must be arbitrary. What I am trying to arrive at is, how do you establish costs in Great Britain? It is done, I suppose, with some relation to what pre-war costs were, and I am trying to find out who it is that actually bears the cost of the ocean-borne traffic which is necessary to service our own troops overseas. Will the minister admit that my contention is correct that pricing is not a scientific business, that the only fair way in ordinary times is what the traffic will bear, with competition keeping the prices reasonable, and that in war time it is fairly well arbitrary. And I am asking him, does it bear any relation to pre-war prices? How do they do it? Frankly, I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext: Ocean rates have been established as universal; they are fixed for Canada and fixed for Britain, and that is an item of fixed cost. War risk insurance rates vary from time to time, depending upon the activity of submarines, and I think it is just as easy to determine the cost of an article to-day as it would be in ordinary times; that is, direct cost. The hon. member speaks of indirect cost, the cost of convoying. Canada is doing about half the convoying on the Atlantic route. I see no reason to believe that Britain's contribution in the matter of convoying is greater than that of Canada. My hon. friend seems determined to make me believe that Britain is getting the worst of the transaction. That has not been my experience in dealing with Britain. But I think they are just as anxious as we are to determine the actual cost. We have experts on the ground there who should be able to agree on a cost which is the real cost. I cannot believe it is unfair to either party.	[DOT]

-for the time being at least, there is one question which arises under this definition section of the united nations Mutual Aid bill; that is the question of Canada's shipping policy or her lack of shipping policy. Paragraph (d) of section 2 defines war supplies, and paragraph (i) of that subsection reads: "any weapon, munition, aircraft or ship".
Which means, I take it, that under the provisions of this bill it will be possible for the Canadian government through the Canadian Mutual Aid board to transfer or give away merchant ships. I believe that at the present time very few of the ships we have been building in Canada are operated by this country, either by the government or an agency thereof or by a private company. I may be wrong in that, but there does not seem to have been any definite shipping policy announced by the government. In any event, the time has come when there should be a shipping policy and it should be definitely made known to the Canadian people.
I say that for several reasons. In the first place, many years ago in the days of wooden ships Canada was both a great shipbuilding country and a great shipping power; one of the great shipping nations of the world. As hon. members know, in those days, the bulk of our shipbuilding was done in the maritime provinces. Then in the last war we did a
Mutual Aid Bill

great deal of shipbuilding, including the building of steel ships. The Department of Munitions and Supply have put out a very interesting publication called "The Industrial Front," which contains production facts revised up to January 1, 1943. At page 64 of that publication we find it stated that in the last war Canada built sixty-three steel ships totaling 380.140 dead-weight tons under the programme started during the great war and completed in 1920. So much for our steel shipbuilding in the last war.
In this war there was quite a long delay in starting to build steel cargo ships. On June 14, 1940, which was after the huns had struck in western Europe, I suggested to the Minister of Munitions and Supply in the house that the time had come for Canada to inaugurate a steel shipbuilding programme, and his reply then was rather remarkable. He said, as reported at page 785 of Hansard of that year:
Whether at a time like this w'e should divert the productive capacity of Canada to the peacetime occupation of building merchant ships is, I think, questionable.
Accordingly, in the summer of 1940 the government declined to take any steps to start building steel ships in Canada. However, later in that year or early in 1941 conditions became so serious with regard to shipping that they decided on a steel shipbuilding programme. Reference to that will be found at page 216 of this booklet, "The Industrial Front", w'here it explains that on April 4, 1941, a government corporation was set up known as Wartime Merchant Shipping Limited whose job was to take charge of the building of steel cargo ships in Canada.
The plan apparently is that this nation shall build 300 steel cargo' ships with a total value of about $500 million. Most of those ships are to be of 10,350 tons.
On March 1 of this year an answer to a question was placed in Hansard showing that at that time or within a few days of that time there had been delivered to the Canadian government ninety-seven cargo ships of 10,350 tons dead-weight carrying capacity and one ship of 4,700 tons, making a total tonnage of over a million. The booklet goes on to show that we have been building ships at a rate equal to the building in Great Britain, and it says that Canada has reached the greatest shipbuilding capacity in her history, in fact, at page 62 it is stated that Canada ranks as one of the world's foremost shipbuilding nations. I think there can be no question of the truth of that fact.
In addition, we have taken up the training of mercb-.nt seamen. The minister can correct
fl
me if I am wrong; but reading from the booklet, "Training for the Merchant Navy", issued by the director of merchant seamen, we find that we have two training schools, one being St. Margaret's sea training school at Hubbards, Nova Scotia, to train men to be junior ordinary seamen, and the other the marine engineering instructional school at Prescott, Ontario, to train men for the duties of trimmers and firemen. I believe we have raised in Canada about 38,000 to 40,000 seamen; those figures I obtained from press dispatches; they may not be entirely accurate, but the minister can give the proper ones when he replies.
That is the position; we are building several hundred of these ships and are training merchant seamen to man them; yet apparently we have been turning over practically all our ships to either Great Britain or the United States, and of those that we do not turn over to those nations many are being operated by the British government or some agency of the British government rather than by'Canada. I believe Canada is operating very few, probably under ten, despite the fact that on April 8, 1942, the government set up a government company known as the Park Steamship Company Limited, whose duties are the control and operation of newly built Canadian cargo vessels.
Apparently, too, when Canada requires shipping for her needs she has to go to the shipping board to which the Minister of Munitions and Supply referred when he spoke the other night as reported at page 2471 of Hansard. I believe further that Canada has no representative on that shipping board, which has its headquarters in Washington. In other words, we have no voice in the allotment of shipping, despite the fact that we produce so many ships.
There is a very large "why" to be answered by the government with regard to this question of shipping. Canada has a background in shipping. We build ships; we train seamen; w'e are a two-ocean nation, bordering on both the Atlantic and the Pacific. We can only live by our exports; we must export goods and will always have to export goods. Such being the facts, it does seem to me that Canada should be not only a great shipbuilding nation but also a great shipping power.
I hope the government have gone much further than I have suggested in my remarks.
I hope I am wrong in my facts, but I do suggest that it is high time Canada had a shipping policy both for the war and for the post-war period; that this is vital to the development of this nation; that the government is wrong in turning over all the ships

maintopic: FALCONBRIDGE NICKEL COMPANY-STATEMENT AS TO OPERATION OF NORWAY REFINERY
speechtext:
Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, there is a matter to which I wish to refer. Recently there appeared in the press a statement by the president of the Falconbridge Nickel company. I did not raise this matter on the orders of the day, because one is pretty well restricted ip what one says at that time, but I think this is a statement of which the government should take notice.
At a meeting of this company in Toronto on, I am told, April 28, the president, during the course of his remarks, is reported to have made a statement which in my opinion is definitely against the best interests of the country and of our war effort. I am going to read the statement as it is reported in the press:
Incidentally you will be glad to hear-as I was-that through indirect channels it is reported that your Norway refinery is safe so far and is being maintained.
It is in operation by your Norwegian staff, under German control, on the same Norwegian nickel-copper ore-production that we formerly handled on toll basis.
It seems to me that a statement of that description ought not to go unchallenged by the government. It is as much as to say that the nickel company and the men who operate it in Norway are operating it with the company's approval, in the midst of a war that is bitter and that is endangering the whole of civilization. I draw this to the attention of
the government because I feel that it is a matter of which note should be taken. I,am sure that if some individual should come to this country from Norway and say "You will be happy to know that our brother is safe and fighting on the side of the Germans," he would be treated immediately as a dangerous and subversive individual. It seems to me that we should not tolerate statements like that to which I refer. Indeed, some of these corporations with their international associations were a menace to our civilization before this war broke out, and it seems altogether probable and likely that even now they are maintaining some association with some of our enemies. We know they did that during the' last war, and we have had reason to fear it is being done in this war. I am not forgetting, of course, that even after the present war had been in progress for months these companies shipped nickel to Japan. Whether or not they did so on contracts made prior to the war, I do not know. It is true that we were at peace with Japan; nevertheless it was quite obvious that events were leading up to a conflict in the Pacific, and I think this parliament and this government should take note of this situation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have one or two other matters I should like to bring up in this connection, and I do not know whether or not to go on with them to-night. Jt is just eleven o'clock, and I believe it would be best to call it that.
